/ad-campaigns/atari-have-you-played: Atari's 1982 "Have You Played Atari Today?" campaign tried to make Atari a generic word for home video gaming.
/ad-campaigns/dreamcast-its-thinking: Sega's $100 million "It's Thinking" campaign backed the Dreamcast's 9.9.99 launch, the most successful console launch to that point.
/ad-campaigns/game-boy-launch: Nintendo sold the Game Boy on Tetris and battery life rather than specs, an approach that beat the colour Lynx and Game Gear.
/ad-campaigns/genesis-does: Michael Katz's "Genesis does what Nintendon't" pitted the Genesis's arcade-like games against the NES, opening the 16-bit console war.
/ad-campaigns/mortal-kombat-mk-is-coming: Acclaim's Mortal Kombat home launch used a hotline, coordinated TV ads and the SNES-versus-Genesis blood row to drive record sales.
/ad-campaigns/nintendo-play-it-loud: Nintendo spent $10 million on Play It Loud, rebranding for teenage boys with skate parks, graffiti, rock and coloured Game Boys.
/ad-campaigns/nintendo-power-launch: Nintendo Power replaced the Fun Club newsletter in 1988 with a 3.6 million-copy first issue, and ran for 24 years as guide and marketing.
/ad-campaigns/playstation-299: At E3 1995, after the Saturn's $399 price, Sony's Steve Race said "two-ninety-nine" and walked off, one of gaming's great moments.
/ad-campaigns/playstation-ur-not-e: Sony's US PlayStation launch used cryptic teasers, rave aesthetics and the taunt "you are not ready" to stand apart from Nintendo and Sega.
/ad-campaigns/sega-blast-processing: Sega named an obscure hardware quirk no game used "Blast Processing", and won the argument in every American playground.
/ad-campaigns/sega-scream: The shouted "SEGA!" that ended Sega's Genesis TV ads became an audio signature of the 16-bit console war, until Sega dropped it around 1995.
/ad-campaigns/segata-sanshiro: To sell the Saturn in Japan, Sega invented a judo master who assaulted anyone not playing it, a campaign that made him a folk hero.
/ad-campaigns/tomb-raider-lara-croft: Eidos sold Tomb Raider through Lara Croft the celebrity, in music videos, fashion shoots and mainstream magazines.
/ad-campaigns/welcome-next-level: Sega's 1992 "Welcome to the Next Level" campaign dropped comparisons with Nintendo to sell the Genesis as gaming's next step.
/arcade-boards/atari-system-1: Atari's cartridge-based System 1 ran Marble Madness, Road Runner and RoadBlasters, letting operators swap games by changing a board.
/arcade-boards/capcom-cps2: Capcom's CPS-2 arcade board hosted Super Street Fighter II Turbo, all three Darkstalkers and the Marvel vs. Capcom series over a decade.
/arcade-boards/capcom-cps3: Capcom's final arcade board, the peak of 2D sprite hardware, ran Street Fighter III and JoJo's Bizarre Adventure on a library of just six games.
/arcade-boards/data-east-deco: Data East's DECO hardware ran Bad Dudes, Heavy Barrel, Robocop and Midnight Resistance, a run of energetic late-1980s action games.
/arcade-boards/hyper-neo-geo-64: SNK's only 3D arcade board was meant to succeed the Neo Geo MVS. It got seven games in two years, none of them hits.
/arcade-boards/irem-m92: Irem's most powerful board ran In the Hunt, Blade Master and R-Type Leo, the visual peak of the company's coin-op output.
/arcade-boards/konami-gx: Konami's main 2D arcade board of the mid-1990s ran Lethal Enforcers II, Salamander 2 and Sexy Parodius on a 32-bit 68EC020.
/arcade-boards/midway-t-unit: Midway's T-Unit ran Mortal Kombat II and NBA Jam, two of the 1990s' highest-grossing arcade games, on a pixel-addressing graphics CPU.
/arcade-boards/namco-system-21: Namco's 1988 "Polygonizer" was built for real-time 3D polygons, debuting with Winning Run three years before Sega's Model 1.
/arcade-boards/namco-system-22: The first arcade board with texture mapping, Namco's System 22 gave the world Ridge Racer and set the visual standard the industry chased.
/arcade-boards/namco-system-86: The Namco System 86 powered Rolling Thunder and Hopping Mappy as Namco moved from its 8-bit boards toward the 16-bit era.
/arcade-boards/nintendo-vs-system: Famicom hardware in an arcade cabinet: Nintendo's coin-op showroom for the console it was about to sell to America.
/arcade-boards/sega-model-1: Sega's first 3D polygon arcade board ran only four games, but Virtua Racing and Virtua Fighter set the direction of 3D arcade gaming.
/arcade-boards/sega-model-3: Built with Lockheed Martin, Sega's Model 3 ran Virtua Fighter 3, Scud Race and Daytona USA 2, far ahead of any home console of its day.
/arcade-boards/sega-naomi: Sega's NAOMI board shared the Dreamcast's architecture and ran Crazy Taxi, Marvel vs. Capcom 2 and Virtua Tennis over an eleven-year life.
/arcade-boards/sega-system-16: Sega's System 16 board ran Shinobi, Altered Beast and Golden Axe, the rich sprite-based 16-bit arcade games of Sega's late-1980s output.
/arcade-boards/sega-system-32: Sega's System 32 bolted Super Scaler pseudo-3D onto a conventional sprite board, using scaling for sheer spectacle rather than racing tricks.
/arcade-boards/sega-x-board: Sega's dual-68000 X Board, built for sprite scaling and rotation, ran After Burner, Thunder Blade and Super Monaco GP.
/arcade-boards/snk-neo-geo-mvs: SNK's Neo Geo MVS hosted 148 games over fourteen years, including Metal Slug, King of Fighters and Samurai Shodown, on hardware matching the home AES.
/arcade-boards/taito-f2: Taito's main arcade board of the late 1980s and early 1990s, running Liquid Kids, Gun Frontier and Grid Seeker with sprite zoom and rotation.
/arcade-boards/williams-defender-hardwar: Williams' 1 MHz bitmap board with no sprite hardware ran Defender, Robotron: 2084, Joust and Sinistar, among the fastest games of the early 1980s.
/bootlegs/7-grand-dad: 7 Grand Dad grafted a Mario sprite onto a Flintstones platformer; a Twitch streamer found it on a multicart in 2014 and made it famous.
/bootlegs/codemasters-unlicensed-nes: Codemasters published unlicensed NES games, including Dizzy titles, through its Camerica label without Nintendo's approval.
/bootlegs/dian-shi-ma-li: A 1989 Taiwan-only Famicom slot-machine game fronted by an off-model Mario, which seeded a genre of Taiwanese gambling bootlegs.
/bootlegs/famiclone-pirate-hardware: Famiclones, unlicensed Famicom copies, spread across Asia, Eastern Europe, South America and Africa from the late 1980s.
/bootlegs/hong-kong-97: A journalist made Hong Kong 97 in a week, with Jackie Chan's face from a film poster and a stolen LaserDisc soundtrack, and sold about thirty.
/bootlegs/kart-fighter: Kart Fighter, an unlicensed Famicom game, put Super Mario Kart's eight racers into a Street Fighter II-style one-on-one brawler.
/bootlegs/pokemon-diamond-jade: Chinese pirates rebranded Telefang as fake Pokémon Diamond and Jade, with incomprehensible English and sabotage that broke saving.
/bootlegs/pokemon-vietnamese-crystal: A pirated Pokémon Crystal translated via Japanese and Chinese into English, so broken it became one of gaming's most quoted scripts.
/bootlegs/squirrel-king-super-mario-worl: A Genesis bootleg that hacked a Chip 'n Dale game with stolen Super Mario All-Stars graphics, with the can-can on its menu.
/bootlegs/street-fighter-ii-rainbow-edit: Rainbow Edition, a notorious bootleg of Champion Edition, added homing fireballs, air specials and character swapping mid-match.
/bootlegs/street-fighter-vi-gba: A bootleg Game Boy Advance cartridge sold as Street Fighter VI, a game that did not exist, held a degraded unauthorised Street Fighter II.
/bootlegs/super-mario-world-famicom: Hummer Team's unlicensed Famicom Super Mario World kept the cape, Yoshi and the overworld map on hardware that should not run it.
/bootlegs/tectoy-master-system-brazil: TecToy, Sega's Brazilian distributor, kept making the Master System and new games for years after Sega ended Western support.
/bootlegs/tengen-tetris: Tengen's unlicensed 1989 NES Tetris reverse-engineered Nintendo's lockout chip under a licence Tengen believed was legitimate.
/bossfights/andross-star-fox-64: Andross, a giant head and hands, is Star Fox 64's multi-phase final boss, with a hidden brain form reached by the hard route.
/bossfights/bowser-super-mario-bros: Bowser guards a false princess at the end of every Super Mario Bros. world until the final showdown in World 8-4.
/bossfights/death-castlevania: Death guards the way to Dracula's keep in Castlevania, a Grim Reaper who fills a narrow corridor with spinning sickles.
/bossfights/dr-wily-mega-man-2: Mega Man 2 ends with Dr. Wily's skull-fronted machine and an alien beaten only with Bubble Lead, then Wily's grovelling surrender.
/bossfights/dracula-castlevania: Castlevania's Count Dracula hurls fireballs, then erupts into a towering demon, a two-phase template the series kept.
/bossfights/emerald-ruby-weapon-ff7: Emerald and Ruby Weapon sit outside Final Fantasy VII's plot, far harder than its final boss and fully optional, so players fight them.
/bossfights/ganon-link-to-the-past: Ganon in A Link to the Past reveals himself behind Agahnim, then plunges the arena into darkness lit only by torches.
/bossfights/ganondorf-ocarina-of-time: Ocarina of Time's Ganondorf fight runs from an organ-lit tower duel to a giant beast battle in a crumbling Hyrule Castle.
/bossfights/kefka-final-fantasy-vi: Kefka is the 16-bit JRPG villain who succeeds: he destroys the world mid-game, rules as a god for a year and must then be stopped.
/bossfights/m-bison-street-fighter-ii: M. Bison closes Street Fighter II with Psycho Power, the Scissor Kick and the Psycho Crusher, the game's apex opponent.
/bossfights/mike-tyson-punch-out: Mike Tyson in Punch-Out!! became shorthand for difficulty, with first-round uppercuts that knock Little Mac down in one hit.
/bossfights/mother-brain-super-metroid: Super Metroid's three-phase Mother Brain fight ends with the Rainbow Beam and the baby Metroid's sacrifice to save Samus.
/bossfights/nemesis-resident-evil-3: Nemesis broke Resident Evil's rules, a rocket-launcher-wielding pursuer that chased Jill Valentine from area to area.
/bossfights/psycho-mantis-metal-gear-sol: Psycho Mantis read players' memory cards, faked a broken TV and could only be beaten by moving the controller to port two.
/bossfights/ridley-metroid: Ridley, the dragon-like Space Pirate leader and Samus Aran's archenemy, is killed and resurrected again and again across Metroid.
/bossfights/sephiroth-final-fantasy-vii: Sephiroth's one-winged final form, backed by "One-Winged Angel", was one of the first JRPG boss fights with sampled vocals.
/bossfights/shao-kahn-mortal-kombat-ii: Shao Kahn, Mortal Kombat II's mocking emperor, punished patience and aggression alike and could beat a full-health fighter in a few blows.
/bossfights/yellow-devil-mega-man: Mega Man's Yellow Devil breaks into blocks, hurls them across the screen and reassembles, with one weak eye. Unless you abuse pause.
/box-art/castlevania-nes: The US Castlevania box shows Simon Belmont before Dracula's castle, for a game Konami of America renamed from Akumajō Dracula.
/box-art/chrono-trigger-snes: Square put Akira Toriyama's art on Chrono Trigger's cover, a snowbound battle scene selling its most ambitious RPG on star power.
/box-art/contra-nes: The US Contra box reused Bob Wakelin's painting of two commandos, made for Ocean's computer ports and inspired by Predator and Rambo.
/box-art/earthbound-snes: EarthBound's US release came in an oversized box with a full-colour strategy guide, one of the most elaborate console packages ever.
/box-art/kirby-angry-western-box: Nintendo gave Kirby a scowl on Western box art he never had in Japan, to make a cute character look tough enough to sell.
/box-art/legend-of-zelda-nes-us: Zelda's black-and-gold US box had a die-cut window showing the gold cartridge inside, a packaging masterstroke.
/box-art/mega-man-2-nes-us: Mega Man 2's US box shows the hero holding an ordinary handgun instead of his arm cannon, an artist's tight-deadline accident.
/box-art/mega-man-nes-us: Mega Man's US cover, drawn in about six hours, shows a man in yellow and blue with a handgun. Inafune blamed it for weak sales.
/box-art/metal-gear-nes-terminator-box: Metal Gear's box art is not Solid Snake but a copy of a still of Michael Biehn as Kyle Reese in The Terminator.
/box-art/metroid-nes-japan: Metroid's US NES box showed an armoured Samus in pixel art and gave nothing away, keeping the ending's reveal that Samus is a woman a surprise.
/box-art/mike-tysons-punch-out-nes: Punch-Out!!'s NES box showed Mike Tyson and Little Mac together, selling its David-versus-Goliath premise before a pixel was seen.
/box-art/ninja-gaiden-nes: Ninja Gaiden's US NES box shows a ninja before a burning city; Nintendo Power named it among its favourite NES designs.
/box-art/phalanx-snes-us: Phalanx, a space shooter, has a US cover of a bearded old man in overalls playing a banjo, a deliberate act of marketing surrealism.
/box-art/sonic-the-hedgehog-genesis: Sonic's Genesis box posed him with the confident attitude Sega was selling: faster, cooler and deliberately the anti-Mario.
/box-art/street-fighter-ii-snes: The SNES Street Fighter II box packed the roster into one explosive composition, among the most recognisable 16-bit covers.
/box-art/super-mario-bros-3-nes-us: Super Mario Bros. 3's US box, Raccoon Mario flying beside a giant red "3", is one of the most recognisable NES covers.
/box-art/super-mario-bros-nes: The Super Mario Bros. box set the visual identity of gaming's most successful series with a simple, instantly legible portrait.
/cabinet-art/after-burner-deluxe: Sega's hydraulic After Burner cockpit tilted, rolled and spun with the on-screen jet, a £4,000 machine that made arcades physical.
/cabinet-art/asteroids-upright: Atari's best-selling cabinet, the black Asteroids upright paired a white vector screen with side art of a ship among asteroids.
/cabinet-art/daytona-usa-deluxe: Sega AM2's Daytona USA debuted the Model 2 board, and its deluxe cabinets linked eight machines for one race.
/cabinet-art/defender-upright: Williams' Defender cabinet used panoramic art of a planet, aliens and the player's ship to capture the game's scrolling scale.
/cabinet-art/dragons-lair-upright: Dragon's Lair's cabinet carried original art from Don Bluth's studio, the style of The Secret of NIMH.
/cabinet-art/galaga-upright: Namco's Galaga cabinet showed detailed alien formations against a starfield, refining the visual language of Space Invaders.
/cabinet-art/gauntlet-four-player-cabine: Gauntlet's cabinet stood four players side by side as Warrior, Valkyrie, Wizard and Elf, each with their own joystick and colour.
/cabinet-art/neo-geo-mvs: SNK's Neo Geo MVS cabinet held up to six game cartridges, with swappable marquees and side art inserts for operators.
/cabinet-art/out-run-deluxe-cabinet: Sega's Out Run cabinet was a moving convertible-shaped simulator, putting a Ferrari, a passenger and a coastline in front of you.
/cabinet-art/pac-man-upright: Namco's yellow Pac-Man cabinet showed Pac-Man and the ghosts in a maze, signalling the game's friendly tone to arcade-goers.
/cabinet-art/robotron-2084-upright: Robotron: 2084's cabinet showed humans fleeing robots across a grid, capturing the game's overwhelming chaos.
/cabinet-art/sega-hang-on-ride-on: Yu Suzuki's 1985 Hang-On came in a motorcycle cabinet players straddled and leaned to steer, launching Sega's body-sensation era.
/cabinet-art/spy-hunter-cabinet: Bally Midway's 1983 Spy Hunter gave players a wheel, a two-speed shifter and weapon buttons, set to the Peter Gunn theme.
/cabinet-art/star-wars-cockpit: Atari's sit-down Star Wars cockpit had a flight yoke, a 25-inch colour vector monitor and Darth Vader looming in its side art.
/cabinet-art/street-fighter-ii-upright: Capcom's Street Fighter II cabinet showed all eight fighters in dynamic poses, selling character variety before a coin went in.
/cancelled/castlevania-resurrection-drea: Castlevania: Resurrection, a 3D Dreamcast game starring Sonia and Victor Belmont, was cancelled by Konami in February 2000.
/cancelled/clay-fighter-63-sequel: Interplay planned a true ClayFighter 63⅓ sequel with a rewritten engine to fix the original's flaws, and it never shipped.
/cancelled/fallout-van-buren: Van Buren was Black Isle's turn-based Fallout 3, cancelled in December 2003 as Interplay collapsed and later echoed in Fallout: New Vegas.
/cancelled/last-soldier-atari: The Last Soldier, a 3D action shooter for the Atari Jaguar by Imagitec Design, was cancelled as Atari collapsed.
/cancelled/prey-3d-realms-original: 3D Realms' original Prey, built on real-time portals far ahead of its hardware, was scrapped for years before a new team released it.
/cancelled/project-dream-n64: Project Dream was Rare's SNES RPG about a boy named Edison that moved to the N64 and was redesigned so much it became Banjo-Kazooie.
/cancelled/propeller-arena-dreamcast: Sega AM2's finished Propeller Arena was pulled in September 2001 when its city dogfights became unthinkable after the 9/11 attacks.
/cancelled/sim-mars-maxis: SimMars was Maxis's planned simulation of founding a Mars colony, following SimEarth and SimCity, cancelled before release.
/cancelled/sonic-mars-32x: Sonic Mars was the first attempt at a fully 3D polygonal Sonic, made for the 32X and abandoned when the add-on collapsed.
/cancelled/sonic-xtreme-saturn: Sonic X-treme, Sega's attempt at a 3D Sonic on the Saturn, went through engine changes and crises for three years before cancellation in 1996.
/cancelled/star-wars-darth-vader-n64: LucasArts began a Shadows of the Empire sequel continuing Dash Rendar's story, then cancelled it as focus moved to The Phantom Menace.
/cancelled/starcraft-ghost: StarCraft: Ghost was announced in 2002, changed developers, lost a platform and slipped for four years before Blizzard shelved it.
/cancelled/starfox-2-snes: Star Fox 2 was finished and bug-tested, then shelved in 1995 to protect the N64's 3D, and stayed officially unreleased for 22 years.
/cancelled/thrill-kill-ps1: Thrill Kill was a finished, ultra-violent four-player PlayStation fighter that EA refused to publish after acquiring Virgin Interactive.
/cancelled/twelve-tales-conker-64: Twelve Tales: Conker 64 was a cute Rare platformer scrapped for looking like every Mario 64 clone, then reborn as Conker's Bad Fur Day.
/cancelled/warcraft-adventures-lord-of-t: Warcraft Adventures, a voiced adventure starring a young Thrall, was cancelled weeks before E3 1998 despite being nearly finished.
/cancelled/zelda-mystical-seed-of-courag: The third Zelda Oracle game was cancelled because linking three games together proved impossible to debug.
/characters/alex-kidd: Big-eared Alex Kidd was Sega's mascot before Sonic, so central to the Master System that his first game was built into later models.
/characters/bomberman: Hudson Soft's bomb-laying hero began in a 1983 computer game and became the face of multiplayer party gaming.
/characters/bowser: Bowser, the fire-breathing King of the Koopas, has kidnapped Princess Peach since 1985 and began on Miyamoto's sketchpad as an ox.
/characters/commander-keen: Billy Blaze, an eight-year-old genius in a football helmet, whose 1990 shareware games showed PCs could scroll and funded id Software.
/characters/crash-bandicoot: Naughty Dog's wild-eyed, crate-smashing marsupial was built as the PlayStation's mascot to rival Mario and Sonic.
/characters/dizzy: Dizzy, an egg with boxing gloves made by the teenage Oliver Twins in 1987, starred in one of Britain's most successful 8-bit series.
/characters/donkey-kong: Nintendo's original villain, the barrel-throwing gorilla Donkey Kong, was reborn as a hero in the Super Nintendo era.
/characters/dr-robotnik: Sonic's egg-shaped arch-enemy, a robotics genius called Eggman in Japan and Dr. Ivo Robotnik in the West until Sonic Adventure joined the names.
/characters/earthworm-jim: Earthworm Jim, an earthworm in a robotic super-suit created by Doug TenNapel in 1994, became a hit game, cartoon and toy line.
/characters/fox-mccloud: Fox McCloud, inspired by Kyoto's Fushimi Inari fox statues, debuted in Star Fox in 1993 and has fought in every Super Smash Bros.
/characters/guybrush-threepwood: Guybrush Threepwood, the hapless would-be pirate of Monkey Island, solves absurd problems with wit and inventory, not a sword.
/characters/kirby: Kirby, the pink puffball who inhales enemies and copies their powers, debuted in 1992 as a young Masahiro Sakurai's creation.
/characters/lara-croft: Lara Croft, the British archaeologist adventurer, became one of gaming's first mainstream celebrities after her 1996 debut.
/characters/mega-man: Dr. Light's robot Mega Man fights Dr. Wily's Robot Masters and copies their weapons, in games known for precision platforming.
/characters/pac-man: Pac-Man, the dot-eating yellow creature fleeing four ghosts, became America's most recognisable game character and an industry's mascot.
/characters/pit-kid-icarus: Pit, the angel who cannot fly, escaped the Underworld in 1986's Kid Icarus and returned years later in Super Smash Bros. Brawl.
/characters/rayman: Rayman's floating hands and feet came from a hardware limitation; he anchored Ubisoft's first great mascot platformer.
/characters/ryu: Ryu, Street Fighter's white-gi'd wanderer, is Capcom's flagship fighter, the archetypal fighting-game hero and origin of the Hadoken.
/characters/samus-aran: Samus Aran, a bounty hunter in a Chozo Power Suit, hunts Space Pirates and Metroids; her 1986 reveal as a woman was a landmark.
/characters/sir-arthur: Sir Arthur of Ghosts 'n Goblins loses his armour at the first hit and fights on in boxer shorts, an iconic image of fragility.
/characters/sub-zero: Mortal Kombat's cryomancer ninja was born from a shortcut: the same digitised actor in a different palette, and an enduring rivalry.
/characters/yoshi: Mario's rideable green dinosaur, introduced in Super Mario World (1990), a companion Miyamoto had wanted since the first Super Mario Bros.
/cheat-codes/age-of-empires-cobra-car: An Age of Empires cheat that spawns a Shelby Cobra sports car, an absurdly fast unit that destroys almost anything.
/cheat-codes/castlevania-iii-passwords: Castlevania III's passwords resume at a stage with the partner and difficulty active when the password was given.
/cheat-codes/earthbound-ness-default-nam: EarthBound's naming shortcut fills in the hero's default name, Ness, and default names for the rest of the party.
/cheat-codes/golden-axe-level-select: Golden Axe's Genesis level select, entered at the character-select screen, picks the starting stage in a port with no saves or passwords.
/cheat-codes/goldeneye-007-cheat-menu: GoldenEye 007's cheat menu offers invincibility, all weapons, Paintball Mode and the notorious DK Mode.
/cheat-codes/gta-iii-wanted-level-clear: A Grand Theft Auto III cheat that instantly clears the wanted level and ends every police pursuit.
/cheat-codes/konami-code-gradius: The Konami Code began in the NES port of Gradius: Kazuhisa Hashimoto added it for testing, and entered while paused it gives the ship full power-ups.
/cheat-codes/metroid-justin-bailey: Metroid's JUSTIN BAILEY password starts Samus without her Power Suit, with most items, in a late-game area.
/cheat-codes/nba-jam-hidden-characters: NBA Jam's codes unlock hidden players including Bill Clinton, Al Gore and Midway staff members.
/cheat-codes/nba-jam-on-fire: Three straight baskets set an NBA Jam player on fire, with unlimited turbo and better shooting until the other team scores.
/cheat-codes/sonic-1-debug-mode: Sonic the Hedgehog's debug mode lets the player place objects anywhere in a level and move Sonic freely.
/cheat-codes/tmnt-iv-turtles-in-time-sta: Turtles in Time's SNES stage select is a Konami-Code-style sequence on Controller 2 that lets the player start from any time period.
/cheat-codes/tomb-raider-all-weapons-che: The original Tomb Raider's PlayStation inventory code gives Lara every weapon and full ammo. The walk-and-flip cheat that makes her explode is Tomb Raider II's.

/collections/hardest-retro-games: Retro games made when difficulty was a feature, to extend arcade play, justify a rental or simply test players to their limit.
/collections/most-influential-games: The games that changed what games could be, introducing mechanics and ideas every later designer had to reckon with.
/collections/nes-defining-games: Ten games that defined the NES: what it was, what it could do and why it mattered to a generation of players.
/collections/snes-defining-games: Ten games at the creative and technical peaks of the Super Nintendo, perhaps the richest library in console history.
/comics/captain-n-comic: Valiant's Captain N comic (1990–1991), from the DiC cartoon, sent a teenager into a Nintendo world with Mega Man, Pit and Simon Belmont.
/comics/doom-comic-1996: Marvel's 1996 Doom one-shot, a promotional giveaway, became an internet meme classic for its absurdly hyperbolic Space Marine.
/comics/egm-comic-strips: Early-1990s magazine comic strips in EGM, GameFan and others satirised games for millions of readers every month.
/comics/howard-and-nester: Nintendo Power's house comic starred real employee Howard Phillips and his sidekick Nester, running from issue one until 1993.
/comics/mortal-kombat-malibu: Malibu Comics published 27 Mortal Kombat issues in 1994–95 across interlocking miniseries such as Blood & Thunder and Battlewave.
/comics/nintendo-comics-system: Valiant's Nintendo Comics System (1990–1991) adapted Super Mario Bros., Zelda, Captain N and more in a short-lived but loved line.
/comics/pokemon-adventures: Pokémon Adventures has run since 1997, covering every generation in manga arcs widely seen as the definitive non-game Pokémon story.
/comics/rockman-megamix-ariga: Hitoshi Ariga's Mega Man manga treats the Robot Masters as characters with inner lives rather than boss-fight obstacles.
/comics/sonic-archie: Archie's Sonic the Hedgehog ran 290 issues from 1993 to 2017, the longest-running video game comic, with a mythology far beyond the games.
/comics/street-fighter-ii-manga-masaomi: Masaomi Kanzaki's 1993 Street Fighter II manga was one of the first Japanese adaptations of Capcom's game to reach English readers.
/comics/super-mario-adventures: Super Mario Adventures ran across Nintendo Power's 1992 issues: a complete manga-styled story of Bowser trying to marry the Princess.
/comics/zelda-link-to-the-past-ishinomor: Nintendo Power serialised a twelve-part A Link to the Past comic by Shotaro Ishinomori, creator of Cyborg 009 and Kamen Rider.
/comics/zelda-manga-himekawa: Akira Himekawa, the duo of A. Honda and S. Nagano, adapted ten Zelda games into manga between 1998 and 2022, giving Link a voice.
/competitive/dwango-doom-1994: Before internet play was practical, ten thousand people paid $9.95 a month to dial a number in Texas and play Doom on DWANGO.
/competitive/electronic-sports-world-cup: The Electronic Sports World Cup began in 2003 at a French theme park with 358 players from 37 countries, a major esports event of its decade.
/competitive/evo-moment-37: With one pixel of health left, Daigo Umehara parried all fifteen hits of Justin Wong's super and won, the most iconic moment in esports.
/competitive/space-invaders-championship: Atari's November 1980 Space Invaders tournament drew over 10,000 players in five cities, widely seen as the first major game competition.
/competitive/starcraft-korea-1998: Organised StarCraft play in South Korea from 1998 created the first true esports ecosystem, with TV broadcasts and salaried pros.
/competitive/us-national-video-game-team: In summer 1983 Twin Galaxies put America's best players on a bus full of arcade machines and sent them on tour as a national team.
/competitive/world-cyber-games-2000: The World Cyber Games, the "Esports Olympics", launched in South Korea in 2000 with 174 players from 17 countries, backed by Samsung.
/composers/akira-yamaoka: Akira Yamaoka composed and designed the sound of Silent Hill, whose industrial noise, trip-hop and melancholy rock frightened players.
/composers/ben-daglish: Ben Daglish was a defining Commodore 64 composer, half of W.E.M.U.S.I.C., writing The Last Ninja, Gauntlet and over a hundred more.
/composers/bobby-prince: Bobby Prince, a Vietnam veteran and lawyer, scored Wolfenstein 3D, Doom and Duke Nukem 3D, the sound of the early first-person shooter.
/composers/chris-huelsbeck: Chris Huelsbeck won a magazine competition as a teenager, then wrote the Turrican soundtracks and music tools the Amiga scene relied on.
/composers/david-whittaker: David Whittaker wrote music in machine code for the C64 and Spectrum, scored Shadow of the Beast and wrote the tune behind "Kernkraft 400".
/composers/david-wise: David Wise composed the Donkey Kong Country trilogy's atmospheric, layered soundtracks to match Rare's pre-rendered visuals.
/composers/frank-klepacki: Frank Klepacki joined Westwood at 17; his "Hell March" for Red Alert beat Trent Reznor's Quake music to PC Gamer's soundtrack award.
/composers/grant-kirkhope: Grant Kirkhope joined Rare in 1995 and wrote the bouncy, adaptive scores of Banjo-Kazooie and Donkey Kong 64, including the DK Rap.
/composers/hirokazu-tanaka: Hirokazu Tanaka scored Metroid and Game Boy Tetris at Nintendo, showing that silence and restraint could be as expressive as melody.
/composers/hiroki-kikuta: Hiroki Kikuta spent two years alone with the SNES sound hardware to make Secret of Mana, one of the finest scores in games.
/composers/hitoshi-sakimoto: Hitoshi Sakimoto gave strategy RPGs an orchestral voice with Ogre Battle, Tactics Ogre and Final Fantasy Tactics, then Vagrant Story.
/composers/jake-kaufman: Jake Kaufman (virt.) scored the Shantae series and Shovel Knight, mastering hardware-accurate chiptune across jazz, metal and orchestral styles.
/composers/jeroen-tel: Jeroen Tel co-founded Maniacs of Noise in 1987 and became a defining Commodore 64 composer with Cybernoid, Myth and Turbo Outrun.
/composers/kenji-yamamoto: Kenji Yamamoto gave Metroid its oppressive, alien sound in Super Metroid and the Prime trilogy, some of it hummed on his ride home.
/composers/kinuyo-yamashita: Kinuyo Yamashita scored Castlevania straight out of university; its "Vampire Killer" became the series' most recurring melody.
/composers/koichi-sugiyama: Koichi Sugiyama scored every mainline Dragon Quest, bringing orchestral arrangements to games decades before it became standard.
/composers/koji-kondo-composer: Koji Kondo, Nintendo's first dedicated composer, wrote the Super Mario Bros. and Legend of Zelda themes and defined Nintendo's sound.
/composers/manami-matsumae: Manami Matsumae wrote nearly all of the original Mega Man's music, including the Cut Man stage, and became a revered chiptune figure.
/composers/michiru-yamane: Michiru Yamane's Symphony of the Night score blended Baroque counterpoint, metal guitar and jazz into the sound of the Metroidvania.
/composers/motoi-sakuraba: Motoi Sakuraba scored Star Ocean, Valkyrie Profile, Golden Sun and Dark Souls among dozens of games over three decades.
/composers/rob-hubbard: Rob Hubbard was the most celebrated Commodore 64 composer, writing Monty on the Run, Commando and dozens more for the SID chip.
/composers/takenobu-mitsuyoshi: Sega's singing composer: he wrote and sang Daytona USA's songs, scored Virtua Racing and Shenmue, and voiced Akira in Virtua Fighter.
/composers/tim-follin: Tim Follin's Spectrum, C64 and NES music pushed 8-bit sound hardware beyond what its engineers designed it to do.
/composers/tim-wright-cold-storage: Tim Wright, as CoLD SToRAGE, scored Psygnosis' Amiga hits and WipEout, whose big-beat soundtrack brought club music into games.
/composers/yoko-shimomura: Yoko Shimomura scored Street Fighter II and Kingdom Hearts, bringing classical training and emotional range to both genres.
/controllers/atari-5200-controller: The Atari 5200 stick had an analogue joystick, keypad and pause button, but it did not re-centre and wore out, and is named among the worst.
/controllers/atari-jaguar-controller: The Jaguar's pad put a 12-key telephone keypad under three face buttons, a bulky design often named one of the worst controllers ever made.
/controllers/atari-paddle-controller: A potentiometer knob sold in pairs with about 330 degrees of travel, the analogue input that made Pong, Breakout and Kaboom! possible.
/controllers/colecovision-controller: Coleco's controller combined a short joystick with a 12-key keypad and game-specific overlays, typical of early-1980s experimentation.
/controllers/dreamcast-controller: The Dreamcast pad paired an analogue stick and analogue triggers with two slots for the VMU and vibration pack, inventive but bulky.
/controllers/game-boy-controls: The Game Boy's d-pad, A, B, Start and Select: a deliberately minimal layout for thumbs, built to survive rough treatment by children.
/controllers/gamecube-controller: A controller built around one enormous green button, with analogue triggers that click at the end of their travel, still used competitively.
/controllers/neo-geo-aes-joystick: The Neo Geo AES shipped with a heavy, microswitched arcade stick and four large buttons, matching SNK's arcade hardware, in the $599 box.
/controllers/nes-advantage: Nintendo's official arcade stick, built by Asciiware, with a microswitched joystick, turbo dials and a slow-motion button.
/controllers/nes-d-pad: Gunpei Yokoi's cross-shaped d-pad, from Game & Watch to the 1983 Famicom pad, replaced joysticks and has governed game control ever since.
/controllers/sega-activator: An octagonal ring that read body movement with infrared beams, the first full-body motion controller and a near-total failure in practice.
/controllers/sega-saturn-pad: The Saturn's six-button pad is considered by fighting game players the finest d-pad controller ever made for arcade-to-home ports.
/controllers/snes-controller: The SNES pad added L and R shoulder buttons and the A, B, X, Y layout, the template every modern controller builds on.
/controllers/super-scope: Nintendo's SNES Super Scope swapped the Zapper's pistol for a shoulder-mounted infrared bazooka, one of the first mainstream wireless peripherals.
/controllers/xbox-duke-controller: The largest controller ever bundled with a major console, named Game Informer's "Blunder of the Year" and replaced by Microsoft within a year.
/controllers/zapper-light-gun: The NES Zapper brought the arcade light gun home with Duck Hunt, becoming one of the best-known game accessories of the 1980s.
/controversies/acclaim-marketing-controv: Acclaim's late-1990s stunts included paying families to name babies Turok and offering to advertise on gravestones.
/controversies/blizzard-hong-kong-2019: Blizzard banned Hearthstone pro Blitzchung and took his prize money after he backed Hong Kong's protests on air, provoking a backlash.
/controversies/carmageddon-bbfc-ban: Carmageddon, which rewarded running over pedestrians, was the first game refused classification by the BBFC, a ban overturned on appeal.
/controversies/columbine-and-doom: After the 1999 Columbine massacre, media and a lawsuit blamed violent games, Doom above all, in the medium's most intense moral panic.
/controversies/custers-revenge: Mystique's 1982 Atari 2600 game Custer's Revenge provoked immediate protests and remains one of the most condemned games ever sold.
/controversies/death-race-1976: Exidy's 1976 Death Race, about running down shrieking gremlins, caused the first public outcry over video game violence.
/controversies/doom-moral-panic: Doom became the focus of moral panic, congressional scrutiny and media blame after acts of violence, most of all Columbine in 1999.
/controversies/grand-theft-auto-1997-mor: The original GTA's moral panic was deliberate: BMG Interactive hired publicist Max Clifford to manufacture the scandal.
/controversies/hot-coffee: A hidden sex minigame in GTA San Andreas's code led to hearings, an AO re-rating, recalls and a $20 million settlement.
/controversies/lara-croft-sexualisation: Lara Croft's success made her the most discussed female game character of the 1990s and the focus of a debate on representation.
/controversies/manhunt-2003: British papers blamed Rockstar's Manhunt for a teenager's murder, until police said the game was found in the victim's room, not the killer's.
/controversies/night-trap-senate-hearing: Night Trap became a 1993 Senate hearing exhibit, described in terms that made the campy, low-budget game sound far more dangerous.
/controversies/phantasmagoria-1995: Roberta Williams' 1995 FMV horror game was banned in Australia and refused by US retailers, yet became Sierra's best seller.
/controversies/postal-1997: Running With Scissors' Postal, about a man committing mass murder in an American town, became a lightning rod for the violence debate.
/controversies/seaman-dreamcast-controve: Seaman, a Dreamcast pet fish with a human face narrated by Leonard Nimoy, drew attention for its microphone play and unsettling tone.
/controversies/wolfenstein-3d-german-ban: Germany banned Wolfenstein 3D for its swastikas under laws against Nazi propaganda, a collision of law, history and art.
/cover-stories/crash-magazine-oliver-fre: Crash's covers were Oliver Frey's hyper-detailed airbrushed paintings, so striking people bought the Spectrum magazine for the art.
/cover-stories/edge-issue-1: Edge's first issue set a new tone for games journalism: analytical, design-focused and willing to give low scores.
/cover-stories/egm-doom-pc-breakthrough: EGM's 1994 feature on Doom's shareware success marked the moment PC gaming began to seriously challenge consoles.
/cover-stories/egm-final-fantasy-vii: EGM's pre-release coverage of Final Fantasy VII, a PlayStation exclusive after Square's SIGGRAPH demo, helped make it a cultural event.
/cover-stories/egm-playstation-reveal: EGM's E3 1995 coverage captured Sony's $299 PlayStation price, announced on stage to undercut the Sega Saturn by $100.
/cover-stories/egm-sheng-long-hoax: EGM's April Fools story invented a hidden Street Fighter II boss, Sheng Long, and the fiction spread worldwide into Capcom's canon.
/cover-stories/electronic-games-issue-1: Before Electronic Games there was no video game magazine; its editors invented words like "playfield", "scrolling" and "screenshot".
/cover-stories/famitsu-first-perfect-sco: Over a decade after adopting four-reviewer scores, Famitsu gave its first perfect 40/40 to Ocarina of Time.
/cover-stories/gamefan-launch: GameFan's November 1992 debut brought full-bleed screenshots, early import coverage and unapologetic enthusiasm to games journalism.
/cover-stories/gamepro-street-fighter-ii: GamePro's coverage of Street Fighter II's SNES arrival documented the most important fighting game release and a key SNES moment.
/cover-stories/next-generation-launch: Next Generation launched in January 1995 covering the industry, not just games, with developer interviews and no bylines.
/cover-stories/nintendo-power-issue-1: Nintendo Power's first issue, with a Super Mario Bros. 2 cover, made it the authoritative guide for North American NES owners.
/cover-stories/nintendo-power-pokemon: Nintendo Power's first big Pokémon feature, ahead of the September 1998 launch, introduced millions of Americans to the phenomenon.
/critics/arnie-katz: Arnie Katz co-founded Electronic Games with Bill Kunkel in 1981 and set the standards of American games journalism for a decade.
/critics/bill-kunkel: Bill Kunkel, "The Game Doctor", co-founded Electronic Games in 1981, the first newsstand video game magazine.
/critics/chris-kohler: Chris Kohler won a Fulbright for studying Japanese game history and now writes the history inside the re-releases themselves.
/critics/dave-halverson: Dave Halverson founded GameFan in 1992 with an enthusiast style that put import coverage and presentation first.
/critics/ed-semrad: Ed Semrad was one of EGM's founding reviewers and its editor through much of the 1990s, its authoritative voice on Nintendo.
/critics/gary-penn: Gary Penn reviewed for Zzap!64, edited The One and was DMA Design's creative director when the first Grand Theft Auto shipped.
/critics/gary-whitta: Gary Whitta helped found PC Gamer in Britain, edited its US edition, then wrote The Book of Eli and co-wrote Rogue One's story.
/critics/jeff-gerstmann: Jeff Gerstmann's 2007 dismissal from GameSpot over alleged advertiser pressure became a defining ethics case; he co-founded Giant Bomb.
/critics/jeff-green: Jeff Green was the last editor-in-chief of Computer Gaming World and helped pioneer the games-magazine podcast.
/critics/jenn-frank: Jenn Frank wrote personal essays on games' emotional and social side for Offworld and The Guardian when such voices were rare.
/critics/kieron-gillen: Kieron Gillen's 2004 New Games Journalism manifesto turned game writing from consumer guidance toward personal, literary experience.
/critics/steven-kent: Steven L. Kent wrote The Ultimate History of Video Games (2001), built from hundreds of original industry interviews.
/critics/tim-rogers: Tim Rogers' hyper-articulate, personal criticism, up to multi-hour video reviews, reinvented what a game review could be.
/decades/1950s: The first computer games of the 1950s were research and exhibition pieces: Bertie the Brain, Nimrod, OXO on EDSAC, and Tennis for Two in 1958.
/decades/1960s: In the 1960s games moved onto university computers: Spacewar! spread between PDP-1s, Hamurabi simulated a city-state, and Ralph Baer began the Odyssey.
/designers/alexey-pajitnov: Alexey Pajitnov created Tetris at a Soviet research institute in 1984, the best-selling puzzle game in history.
/designers/andrew-braybrook: Andrew Braybrook's Paradroid and Uridium set the Commodore 64 standard, and his Zzap!64 diaries showed readers how games were made.
/designers/dani-bunten-berry: Dani Bunten Berry designed M.U.L.E. and The Seven Cities of Gold, building her games around shared play decades before it was common.
/designers/david-crane: David Crane co-founded Activision and designed Pitfall! for the Atari 2600, then made Ghostbusters and A Boy and His Blob.
/designers/fumito-ueda: Fumito Ueda directed Ico and Shadow of the Colossus through "design by subtraction", removing everything that was not essential.
/designers/gunpei-yokoi: Gunpei Yokoi invented the Game Boy and Game & Watch and produced Metroid, defining Nintendo's "lateral thinking with withered technology".
/designers/hideo-kojima: Hideo Kojima created Metal Gear and the stealth genre, mixing cinematic storytelling with postmodern design over four decades.
/designers/hironobu-sakaguchi: Hironobu Sakaguchi created Final Fantasy and guided its first decade, shaping the Japanese RPG into a cinematic storytelling medium.
/designers/howard-scott-warshaw: Howard Scott Warshaw made Yars' Revenge, Raiders of the Lost Ark and E.T., written in five weeks, then became a psychotherapist.
/designers/jeff-minter: Jeff Minter: forty years of psychedelic shooters full of llamas, camels and sheep, from Gridrunner on the VIC-20 to Tempest 2000.
/designers/john-carmack: John Carmack wrote the engines behind Wolfenstein 3D, Doom and Quake, the technical foundations of the first-person shooter.
/designers/john-romero: John Romero designed the levels and feel of Wolfenstein 3D, Doom and Quake, the spatial language of the first-person shooter.
/designers/jordan-mechner: Jordan Mechner created Karateka and Prince of Persia, whose rotoscoped animation brought film-like movement to computer games.
/designers/kazunori-yamauchi: Kazunori Yamauchi made Gran Turismo, the PlayStation's "real driving simulator", and became a Nürburgring endurance racer.
/designers/kenji-eno: Kenji Eno founded Warp and made D, Enemy Zero and an audio-only game playable without sight, along with famously theatrical stunts.
/designers/koji-igarashi: Koji "IGA" Igarashi co-directed Symphony of the Night, led Castlevania for a decade and crowdfunded Bloodstained with $5.5 million.
/designers/masahiro-sakurai: Masahiro Sakurai joined HAL at nineteen, created Kirby by twenty-two and invented Super Smash Bros. from an unrelated prototype.
/designers/mike-singleton: Former teacher Mike Singleton wrote The Lords of Midnight and Midwinter, vast explorable worlds on 8-bit and 16-bit computers.
/designers/peter-molyneux: Peter Molyneux created Populous, Theme Park and Black & White, pioneering the god game and moral choice as a game system.
/designers/richard-garriott: Richard Garriott, Lord British, created Ultima and brought virtue and ethics into the role-playing game.
/designers/ron-gilbert: Ron Gilbert co-created Maniac Mansion, invented SCUMM, directed The Secret of Monkey Island and wrote "Why Adventure Games Suck".
/designers/satoshi-tajiri: Satoshi Tajiri turned a childhood love of insect collecting into Pokémon, the highest-grossing media franchise in history.
/designers/shigeru-miyamoto: Shigeru Miyamoto created Donkey Kong, Super Mario Bros. and The Legend of Zelda, the foundation of platformer and adventure game design.
/designers/shinji-mikami: Shinji Mikami joined Capcom via a job-fair flyer, made a Disney platformer, then directed Resident Evil and defined survival horror.
/designers/sid-meier: Sid Meier created Civilization, Pirates! and Railroad Tycoon, defining strategy simulation and "just one more turn" design.
/designers/tokuro-fujiwara: Tokuro Fujiwara made Commando, Ghosts 'n Goblins and Bionic Commando, produced Mega Man and made Sweet Home, Resident Evil's basis.
/designers/tomohiro-nishikado: Tomohiro Nishikado made Space Invaders alone, its art, sound, code and the arcade hardware he built because none could run it.
/designers/yoshiki-okamoto: Yoshiki Okamoto designed Time Pilot and Gyruss, directed 1942 and produced Final Fight and Street Fighter II, then made Monster Strike.
/designers/yoshio-sakamoto: Yoshio Sakamoto shaped Metroid's characters, the Famicom Detective Club and Super Metroid, then WarioWare and Rhythm Heaven.
/designers/yu-suzuki: Yu Suzuki directed Hang-On, Space Harrier, Out Run, Virtua Fighter and Shenmue, pioneering arcade hardware and open-world storytelling.
/designers/yuji-horii: Yuji Horii invented the Japanese console RPG with Dragon Quest and was the first game creator awarded the Order of the Rising Sun.
/designers/yuji-naka: Yuji Naka programmed the original Sonic the Hedgehog, co-founded Sonic Team and directed NiGHTS into Dreams.
/developers/apogee: Apogee pioneered shareware, giving away episode one and selling the rest by mail, published Wolfenstein 3D and built Duke Nukem.
/developers/broderbund: Broderbund published Karateka and Prince of Persia, co-published Myst and turned Carmen Sandiego into games, TV and classroom staple.
/developers/chunsoft: Koichi Nakamura's Chunsoft programmed the first five Dragon Quest games, invented the sound novel and began the Mystery Dungeon series.
/developers/cinematronics: Cinematronics released the first commercial vector game, Space Wars, made Star Castle and published the laserdisc hit Dragon's Lair.
/developers/compile: Compile made fast shooters such as Zanac, Aleste and MUSHA, then invented Puyo Puyo, the hit that outlived the company.
/developers/data-east: Data East made BurgerTime, Karate Champ and Bad Dudes, invented the interchangeable arcade board and was a major pinball maker.
/developers/irem: Irem made Kung-Fu Master, the parallax-scrolling Moon Patrol and R-Type, widely ranked the finest horizontal shoot 'em up.
/developers/lucasarts: LucasArts made Maniac Mansion, Monkey Island, Day of the Tentacle and Grim Fandango, then abandoned adventure games and closed in 2013.
/developers/namco: Namco created Pac-Man, Galaga and Dig Dug and pioneered arcade hardware before expanding into home console publishing.
/developers/nihon-falcom: Japan's Nihon Falcom made Dragon Slayer, Xanadu and Ys, laying foundations of the action RPG with some of the 1980s' best FM music.
/developers/origin: Origin Systems created Ultima, Wing Commander and Ultima Online, defining the computer RPG and the space combat sim.
/developers/psygnosis: Psygnosis defined the Amiga's look with Roger Dean art and showpiece games, then helped launch the PlayStation in Europe with Wipeout.
/developers/quintet: Quintet made ActRaiser, Soul Blazer, Illusion of Gaia and Terranigma for Enix, action RPGs remembered for philosophical, dark themes.
/developers/sega: Sega rose from coin-op machines to challenge Nintendo, producing Sonic the Hedgehog, Virtua Fighter and five generations of home consoles.
/developers/square: Square made Final Fantasy as a last gamble before bankruptcy, then built the defining JRPG series plus Chrono Trigger and Secret of Mana.
/developers/the-bitmap-brothers: The London studio behind Xenon 2, Speedball 2, Gods and The Chaos Engine, classics of the 16-bit Amiga era.
/developers/westwood: Westwood Studios created Dune II, the template for real-time strategy, then built Command & Conquer into a defining 1990s PC series.
/difficulty/battletoads-turbo-tunnel: Battletoads is often called the hardest NES game, and its Turbo Tunnel speeder bike stage ended most players' runs.
/difficulty/castlevania-ii-simons-quest: Simon's Quest hid its progress behind NPC hints so cryptic, mistranslated or false that players needed outside help to finish.
/difficulty/castlevania-nes: Castlevania's knockback flung Simon Belmont backwards when hit, often off ledges into pits, making its platforming a test of nerve.
/difficulty/contra-nes: Contra on NES gave three lives and few continues for eight stages of relentless fire and one-hit deaths.
/difficulty/ducktales-nes: Capcom's colourful DuckTales hid tight pogo-cane precision, boss patterns that punish hesitation and a tough Moon stage.
/difficulty/ecco-the-dolphin: Ecco the Dolphin looked tranquil but became one of the 16-bit era's hardest games, with puzzles the game barely explained.
/difficulty/ghosts-n-goblins-nes: Ghosts 'n Goblins made players finish the whole game twice for the true ending, revealing this only after the final boss.
/difficulty/ghouls-n-ghosts-genesis: Ghouls 'n Ghosts kept two-hit deaths and the double-completion requirement, adding armour, uneven new weapons and hard levels.
/difficulty/ikaruga: Treasure's Ikaruga demands dodging dense bullets while switching black and white polarity to absorb same-coloured fire.
/difficulty/kid-icarus-nes: Kid Icarus puts its cruellest stretch first, a vertically scrolling Underworld where falling off the screen means death.
/difficulty/mega-man-nes: The original Mega Man had no saves or passwords; switching off meant starting over through six Robot Masters and Wily's castle.
/difficulty/ninja-gaiden-nes: Ninja Gaiden's final stage sent players back to Act 6-1 if they died on any of its three bosses, a famously cruel design.
/difficulty/r-type-arcade: Irem's R-Type tests memory, not reflexes: every enemy spawns in the same place every time, and the first time will kill you.
/difficulty/silver-surfer-nes: Silver Surfer kills the player on contact with any wall, floor, ceiling or projectile, in levels packed with obstacles.
/difficulty/super-ghouls-n-ghosts-snes: Super Ghouls 'n Ghosts is often called the SNES's hardest game and demands players beat it twice for the real ending.
/difficulty/tmnt-nes-dam: Konami's TMNT is remembered for its underwater dam level, defusing bombs past electric seaweed against the clock.
/difficulty/zelda-ii-adventure-of-link: Zelda II swapped top-down play for side-scrolling combat and RPG levelling and is widely called the hardest Zelda game.
/disappointments/atari-5200: The Atari 5200 undermined its power with a non-centring joystick and no backward compatibility with the 2600's library.
/disappointments/castlevania-64: Castlevania 64 took the series into 3D two years after Symphony of the Night redefined it, and struggled in the comparison.
/disappointments/deus-ex-invisible-war: Deus Ex's sequel was built to run on Xbox, so levels shrank, the skill system vanished and ammunition became universal.
/disappointments/duke-nukem-forever: Duke Nukem Forever spent fifteen years in development hell and arrived in 2011 feeling a decade out of date.
/disappointments/earthworm-jim-3d: Earthworm Jim 3D lost the 2D games' tight controls and visual invention, becoming a sluggish 3D platformer.
/disappointments/enter-the-matrix: Enter the Matrix had an hour of Wachowski-shot footage and sold five million copies, yet an EGM reviewer called it glaringly unfinished.
/disappointments/et-atari-2600: Given five and a half weeks, Howard Scott Warshaw made E.T., the symbol of the 1983 crash, later dug up from a New Mexico landfill.
/disappointments/mega-man-6: Mega Man 6 arrived in 1993 after the series and NES had peaked: technically polished but creatively exhausted.
/disappointments/star-fox-adventures: Star Fox Adventures turned Rare's Dinosaur Planet into a Star Fox game at Nintendo's request, an awkward fit for both.
/disappointments/tomb-raider-angel-of-da: Angel of Darkness was cut down and forced out unfinished by a cash-hungry publisher, nearly killing Tomb Raider and ending Core's run.
/disappointments/ultima-viii-pagan: Ultima VIII turned the Avatar into a platform hero and shipped, its creator admitted, three months unfinished: "Super Avatar Brothers".
/disappointments/zelda-ii-adventure-of-l: Zelda II traded the original's free top-down exploration for side-scrolling action RPG play, discarding much of what players loved.
/easter-eggs/diablo-2-secret-cow-level: Diablo II's Secret Cow Level of club-wielding cows was Blizzard's answer to a fan rumour from the first game.
/easter-eggs/donkey-kong-country-2-lost-: Donkey Kong Country 2's Lost World is hidden under Crocodile Isle behind a toll of 75 Kremkoins from bonus rooms.
/easter-eggs/doom2-romero-head: Doom II's final boss hides the impaled head of id co-founder John Romero behind its wall, and shooting it is the only way to win.
/easter-eggs/doom2-wolfenstein-keen: Doom II's two secret levels rebuild Wolfenstein 3D stages, ending with four hanged Commander Keens that must be shot to finish.
/easter-eggs/earthbound-anti-piracy: EarthBound detects pirated copies, makes the game harder and deletes every save at the final boss.
/easter-eggs/final-fantasy-vii-w-item-du: Cancelling the second pick with W-Item materia in Final Fantasy VII duplicates items, giving endless Megalixirs.
/easter-eggs/goldeneye-007-paintball-mod: GoldenEye 007's Paintball Mode cheat replaces bullet impacts with bright paint blobs, wildly at odds with its spy-thriller tone.
/easter-eggs/konami-code-gradius: Up, Up, Down, Down, Left, Right, Left, Right, B, A in Gradius grants full power-ups, the origin of gaming's most famous cheat.
/easter-eggs/metal-gear-solid-psycho-man: Psycho Mantis reads the player's memory card and moves the controller; beating him means plugging it into the second port.
/easter-eggs/metroid-justin-bailey: Metroid's JUSTIN BAILEY password starts near the end with most power-ups and shows Samus Aran without her Power Suit.
/easter-eggs/nba-jam-hidden-characters: NBA Jam hides playable Bill Clinton, Al Gore, Prince Charles and Midway staff, unlocked by entering initials and buttons.
/easter-eggs/super-mario-64-yoshi-roof: Collect all 120 stars in Super Mario 64 and Yoshi waits on Peach's Castle roof with 100 lives and a message from the team.
/easter-eggs/super-mario-bros-minus-worl: A wall-clipping trick in Super Mario Bros. reaches World -1, an endless underwater loop that can never be completed.
/easter-eggs/the-sims-tragic-clown: The Sims' cursed Tragic Clown painting drags a household's mood down and summons the sad clown himself.
/easter-eggs/wolfenstein-3d-pac-man-leve: A hidden Wolfenstein 3D level recreates a Pac-Man maze in first-person 3D, complete with the ghosts.
/endings/aerith-death-final-fantasy-vii: Midway through Final Fantasy VII, Sephiroth kills Aerith without warning, a moment that changed what games could do emotionally.
/endings/baldurs-gate-twist-ending: Baldur's Gate reveals the hero is a child of Bhaal, dead god of murder, and that the villain Sarevok is their half-sibling.
/endings/castlevania-sotn-inverted-castl: After an apparent final boss, Symphony of the Night reveals its real ending needs Dracula's castle beaten again, upside down.
/endings/chrono-trigger-multiple-endings: Chrono Trigger was the first mainstream JRPG with multiple endings, thirteen in all, set by when the player fought the final boss.
/endings/final-fantasy-vi-final-sequence: Final Fantasy VI ends with a three-team assault on Kefka's tower, a final fight to "Dancing Mad" and a feature-length escape.
/endings/ghosts-n-goblins-loop-ending: Beat Ghosts 'n Goblins and you learn the victory was Satan's trap, and must play the whole game again to reach the real ending.
/endings/half-life-g-man-ending: Half-Life ends with the mysterious G-Man offering Gordon Freeman a choice: work for unnamed masters or be abandoned to die.
/endings/metal-gear-solid-2-s3-ending: Metal Gear Solid 2 ends by revealing the colonel guiding you is software and the whole mission was an exercise in controlling information.
/endings/metal-gear-solid-endings-psycho: Metal Gear Solid's Psycho Mantis reads the player's memory card and comments on their games, one of gaming's boldest fourth-wall breaks.
/endings/resident-evil-helicopter-escape: Resident Evil's ending depends on which S.T.A.R.S. members survived and the choices made, ending in an explosion and helicopter rescue.
/endings/shenmue-unresolved-cliffhanger: Shenmue was chapter one of a sixteen-chapter saga; chapter two was cut, the Dreamcast died and the story stopped on a cliffhanger.
/endings/silent-hill-multiple-endings: Silent Hill's endings, from tragic to hopeful, hinge on hidden conditions, and began the series' tradition of a joke UFO ending.
/endings/sonic-cd-good-bad-ending: Sonic CD was the first Sonic with a branching ending, decided by whether players destroyed the robot generators in every level.
/endings/star-fox-64-true-ending: Reaching Andross by Star Fox 64's hard route unlocks the true ending, where Fox's long-dead father James guides him out of the base.
/endings/super-metroid-escape-samus-reve: Super Metroid ends with the baby Metroid's sacrifice, a timed escape from collapsing Zebes and, for fast players, Samus without her suit.
/endings/xenogears-disc-2-ending: Xenogears ran out of production time, so most of its second disc has characters narrate the plot from a chair over a slideshow.
/essays: Long-form essays on retro gaming history, technology and culture: the golden age of arcades and the designers who shaped the medium.
/essays/amiga-mod-music: The Amiga's four-channel sampler spawned the MOD format, letting a global community of composers share and build on each other's work.
/essays/arcade-hardware: Every golden-age arcade game ran on custom hardware. What was inside the cabinet explains why the games looked and felt as they did.
/essays/atari-lynx-story: The Atari Lynx had 1989's best handheld hardware by far, but hardware superiority could not overcome its price.
/essays/capcom-golden-decade: From 1987 to 1997 Capcom made Mega Man, Street Fighter II, Final Fight, Ghouls 'n Ghosts and Resident Evil.
/essays/cd-rom-revolution: Cartridges held 4 to 8 megabytes; CD-ROMs held 650. The jump brought voice acting, orchestral music and cinematic cutscenes.
/essays/cheat-codes-culture: The Konami Code appeared in 1986 and became gaming's most famous sequence; the culture of cheats shaped how people played.
/essays/checkpoint-design: Checkpoints began as a side effect of stage-based games and became how designers set the price of death.
/essays/chris-sawyer-assembly: In 1999 Chris Sawyer wrote RollerCoaster Tycoon in assembly language, because the simulation he wanted would not run any other way.
/essays/chrono-trigger-dream-team: Chrono Trigger (1995) was made by a team so pedigreed the Japanese press called it the Dream Team before release.
/essays/commodore-64-bedroom-coding: The Commodore 64 sold 17 million units from 1982 to 1994, and its open design and manual fostered a generation of bedroom coders.
/essays/copper-raster-effects: A CRT draws one line at a time, and changing the graphics chip between lines let different parts of the screen use different settings.
/essays/copy-protection-era: Before DRM servers and online activation, publishers fought piracy with physical objects: cardboard dials, plastic prisms and booklets of lies.
/essays/dona-bailey: Dona Bailey joined Atari's coin-op division in 1980 as its first woman programmer, and her game became one of its best sellers.
/essays/donkey-kong-country-cgi: Donkey Kong Country (1994) seemed impossible: pre-rendered 3D graphics on ageing 16-bit hardware. This is how Rare did it.
/essays/doom-modding-community: Doom kept its content in WAD files apart from the engine, a decision that let players build new levels and founded modding.
/essays/dungeon-crawler-origins: The dungeon crawler grew from 1970s university mainframe games, through Wizardry and Ultima, into a foundation of Japanese RPGs.
/essays/early-pc-gaming: The IBM PC was built for spreadsheets, not games; becoming a gaming platform took a decade of clever workarounds.
/essays/ed-logg: Ed Logg made three landmark arcade games in three different shapes, connected not by a style but by a method.
/essays/esports-rise: Competitive gaming began with the first high-score boards; this is how it became a professional spectator sport.
/essays/famicom-disk-system: In 1986 Nintendo added a disk drive to the Famicom and kiosks across Japan where players could have new games written onto their disks.
/essays/fighting-game-depth: Fighting games have the steepest learning curve of any major genre. Is that steepness a flaw or a feature?
/essays/final-fantasy-name-origin: Square really did face bankruptcy in 1987 and Final Fantasy really did save it, but the popular story of its name is not right.
/essays/final-fantasy-vii-making: Final Fantasy VII (1997) came from a production crisis, a platform switch, a 200-person team and pre-rendered backgrounds.
/essays/fmv-game-craze: Early-1990s full-motion video games promised interactive cinema; the technology delivered video but not the game.
/essays/game-camera: The camera is the player's relationship to the game world, and every choice about what to show and hide is a design decision.
/essays/game-engine-licensing: For most of gaming history every studio built its own engine, until licensed engines let studios build on others' technology.
/essays/game-preservation-crisis-2: An estimated 87% of classic games are out of print and legally inaccessible, stranded by copyright terms designed for books.
/essays/gaming-magazines-print-era: Gaming magazines were the infrastructure through which gaming culture was transmitted and argued over before the internet.
/essays/gunpei-yokoi: Gunpei Yokoi invented the Game & Watch, the D-pad, the Game Boy and Metroid, using mature technology in new ways.
/essays/how-amiga-worked: How the Amiga managed thousands of colours, four channels of sampled audio, accelerated 2D and multitasking in 1985.
/essays/how-playstation-worked: The PlayStation was designed around one insight: 3D polygon rendering was the future, and the GPU should be built to accelerate it.
/essays/how-snes-worked: The SNES CPU ran at 3.58 MHz against the Genesis's 7.67 MHz, so Nintendo leaned on specialised co-processor chips.
/essays/hub-world-design: A hub world connects other game spaces, and designing one is a different challenge from designing levels.
/essays/hub-world-evolution: The hub world, a central space linking self-contained levels, was 3D game design's answer to replacing the linear stage.
/essays/infocom-text-adventures: Infocom's Zork and its successors made interactive fiction a literary form, with the Z-machine and a devoted audience.
/essays/invention-of-difficulty: How games handle failure is a fundamental design choice; the history of difficulty is the industry learning what players will accept.
/essays/isometric-projection: Before polygons and texture mapping, a handful of developers found that isometric projection could suggest a 3D world.
/essays/japanese-vs-american-arcade: The arcade meant different things in Japan and America, and those differences produced different games and social norms.
/essays/john-carmack: John Carmack's graphics engines defined PC gaming for a decade. This essay looks at what he built, and why he kept discarding it.
/essays/jordan-mechner: Jordan Mechner made Karateka at nineteen and Prince of Persia at twenty-four, both built on characters that move like real people.
/essays/jrpg-goes-west: Japanese RPGs spent most of the 1980s invisible to the West; this is how they went from niche curiosity to mainstream.
/essays/julian-gollop-xcom: X-COM began as Laser Squad 2, a two-player tactical demo on the Atari ST, and shipped after thirty months and a year of overrun.
/essays/kill-screen-integer-overflow: Pac-Man and Donkey Kong have no ending; after hours of perfect play an eight-bit counter runs out of room and the game breaks.
/essays/konami-at-its-peak: From 1987 to 1995 Konami made more NES classics than any other third party: Contra, Castlevania, Gradius and Turtles among them.
/essays/lan-party: The LAN party existed because graphics outran networks: Doom and Quake were too fast for a 28.8k modem, so players brought their PCs.
/essays/lemmings-design: Lemmings (1991) gave players responsibility for dozens of creatures instead of one character, a puzzle game with emotional stakes.
/essays/lucasarts-adventure-games: From 1987 to 1998 LucasArts made Maniac Mansion, Monkey Island, Day of the Tentacle and Sam & Max, a golden run of adventures.
/essays/making-of-doom: In 1993 John Carmack, John Romero and a small id Software team released Doom and rewrote the technical and cultural rules.
/essays/mascot-marketing-wars: The early-1990s Sega-Nintendo rivalry was fought through mascots designed to embody each company's identity.
/essays/metroidvania: The Metroidvania, named for Metroid and Symphony of the Night, is built around a connected world that opens as the player grows.
/essays/metroidvania-template: "Metroidvania" fuses Metroid (1986) and Symphony of the Night (1997), a genre built on a single design principle.
/essays/mode7-illusion-of-3d: Mode 7 let the SNES rotate and scale a background layer, a hardware feature that created the illusion of a 3D world.
/essays/mortal-kombat-esrb: Mortal Kombat's 1993 home release triggered congressional hearings, a Senate investigation and rival rating systems.
/essays/mouse-keyboard-gaming: Game genre is partly determined by input, and the mouse and keyboard shaped the genres that dominated 1990s PC gaming.
/essays/msx-japan-computer: Announced in 1983 as a standard uniting fourteen Japanese makers, the MSX was Microsoft's attempt to do for computers what VHS did.
/essays/n64-cartridge-decision: In 1996 Nintendo launched the N64 on cartridges while the PlayStation was already showing the advantages of CD.
/essays/nes-hardware: The NES was not the most powerful console of its era but the most carefully designed for game development, lockout chip included.
/essays/nolan-bushnell: Nolan Bushnell founded Atari in 1972 with $250 and sold it four years later for $28 million. What happened in between defined an industry.
/essays/origins-of-online-gaming: Networked multiplayer gaming predates the consumer internet by two decades; its history is people connecting computers to play.
/essays/parallax-scrolling: Move the background slower than the foreground and a flat scene gains depth: the principle behind parallax scrolling in games.
/essays/physics-in-games: Game physics, simulating real-world behaviour in interactive worlds, went from novelty to standard expectation remarkably fast.
/essays/platformer-history: The platformer is gaming's most fundamental genre, invented gradually by several designers arriving at similar ideas independently.
/essays/pokemon-cultural-phenomenon: Pokémon Red and Green launched in Japan in February 1996, sold about ten million there and reached North America in September 1998.
/essays/procedural-generation: Procedural generation, creating content by algorithm instead of by hand, is one of game design's most powerful and misunderstood tools.
/essays/ps1-texture-warping: The PS1's distinctive wobble is two separate failures, including textures that swim because of what the GPU could not do.
/essays/publisher-wars-1990s: The 1990s games industry consolidated around a few big publishers, built on annual sports games and aggressive business models.
/essays/rare-nintendo-partnership: Rare went from ZX Spectrum bedroom coding to NES licence work, Nintendo's key second party and Microsoft's costly acquisition.
/essays/rating-system-wars: In 1993 senators Joe Lieberman and Herbert Kohl held hearings on game violence, giving the industry ninety days to regulate itself.
/essays/richard-garriott: Richard Garriott created Ultima, one of gaming's most important RPG series, and used it to explore virtue and ethics.
/essays/rise-of-id-software: id Software released Doom in 1993 and changed the industry in three ways at once, a story rooted in the PC of the time.
/essays/roguelike-randomness-design: Rogue (1980) generated random dungeons and killed characters for good, design principles that remain hugely influential.
/essays/ron-gilbert: Ron Gilbert's adventure philosophy of no dead ends, no unwinnable states and logical puzzles began as a critique of the genre.
/essays/rpg-western-vs-japanese: CRPGs and JRPGs share Dungeons & Dragons ancestry but split into distinct genres, one prizing systemic depth and player freedom.
/essays/satoshi-tajiri: Pokémon was not a commercial calculation but Satoshi Tajiri's attempt to recreate his childhood of collecting insects in rural Japan.
/essays/save-systems-death-design: The save system is one of game design's least discussed but most consequential choices: anywhere, at fixed points, or never.
/essays/sega-story: Sega came within striking distance of beating Nintendo in the 1990s. How it got there, and why it failed, is one of gaming's great stories.
/essays/sega-super-scaler: Hang-On, Space Harrier and OutRun looked like nothing else in 1985, because Sega's hardware scaled sprites in three dimensions.
/essays/shareware-revolution: From 1990 to 1994, giving games away and selling the rest by mail turned PC gaming from a niche hobby into an industry.
/essays/shoot-em-up-grammar: The shoot 'em up is gaming's oldest surviving genre; from Space Invaders to DoDonPachi, shoot, dodge and destroy stayed constant.
/essays/sid-meier: Sid Meier designed Pirates!, Railroad Tycoon and Civilization; his idea that a game is a series of interesting decisions explains them all.
/essays/simcity-god-game: Publishers rejected SimCity (1989) because it had no way to win; Maxis's persistence created a new kind of game.
/essays/skill-tree-design: The skill tree, where early choices decide later options, is the main way games let players shape a character's growth.
/essays/snes-rpg-golden-age: From 1990 to 1996 Square made an unmatched run of SNES RPGs, from Final Fantasy IV, V and VI to Chrono Trigger.
/essays/sound-chip-history: 8-bit and 16-bit game music was written for specific silicon, chips with specific voices and limits.
/essays/sound-golden-age: 1980s game music came from extraordinarily limited hardware, and the composers who worked within those limits wrote unforgettable music.
/essays/speedrunning: Speedrunning began with arcade high-score boards and grew into a systematic practice of finding and exploiting every shortcut.
/essays/sprite-flicker-slowdown: Why NES characters strobed in and out of view on busy screens, and why the whole game lurched into slow motion.
/essays/stealth-game-design: Stealth games build tension through information asymmetry: the player knows more about the guards than the guards know about them.
/essays/tetris-rights-saga: Alexey Pajitnov created Tetris in 1984 and owned none of it. A chain of licences sold by people who did not hold them followed.
/essays/tim-sweeney: Tim Sweeney set out to write a text editor, wrote a game inside it, shipped it as shareware from his parents' house and built Epic.
/essays/tomb-raider-phenomenon: Tomb Raider (1996) introduced Lara Croft, a game character who immediately existed as a cultural figure beyond the game.
/essays/toru-iwatani: Toru Iwatani designed Pac-Man to differ from every other 1980 arcade game, with deliberate choices such as no violence and no death imagery.
/essays/tutorial-problem: Teaching players how to play is one of game design's hardest problems; the history of tutorials shows what works and what doesn't.
/essays/ultima-open-world: Richard Garriott's Ultima invented the persistent world with ethical stakes, NPC schedules and consequences for the player.
/essays/video-game-music-concerts: Game music went from technical afterthought to concert hall repertoire in three decades, from Game Boy bleeps to live orchestras.
/essays/voice-acting-in-games: Games were text-based for two decades not by choice but because storage and processing made voice acting impractical.
/essays/warren-spector: Warren Spector's career at Origin, Looking Glass and Ion Storm traces the rise of the immersive sim and its systemic simulation.
/essays/warren-spector-immersive-sim: Warren Spector's career, from Ultima to System Shock to Deus Ex, follows a single sustained argument about what makes games meaningful.
/essays/yuji-naka: Sonic the Hedgehog (1991) was as much an engineering achievement as a design one; this is what Yuji Naka built and how.
/failed-consoles/3do: An open-licence console launched at $699.99, twice the price of its rivals, that never built the software library needed to justify the cost.
/failed-consoles/atari-5200: The Atari 2600's powerful successor, crippled by joysticks that did not re-centre, no backward compatibility and the 1983 crash.
/failed-consoles/atari-lynx: The first handheld with a colour, backlit screen and sprite scaling, beaten by the Game Boy's software library and battery life.
/failed-consoles/casio-loopy: Casio's 1995 32-bit console for girls, whose defining feature was a built-in colour printer for turning screenshots into stickers.
/failed-consoles/coleco-adam: Coleco's all-in-one computer bundled a printer, tape drives and word processor, then shipped late, broke often and pushed Coleco toward bankruptcy.
/failed-consoles/commodore-cdtv: An Amiga 500 in a black hi-fi case with a CD-ROM drive and no floppy drive, sold for $999 to buyers who never knew what it was for.
/failed-consoles/emerson-arcadia-2001: A $99 console from 1982 whose ready ports of Pac-Man, Galaxian and Defender were never released because of Atari's licences.
/failed-consoles/fm-towns-marty: Released in February 1993, Fujitsu's FM Towns Marty was the world's first 32-bit home console. It arrived first and sold almost nothing.
/failed-consoles/gizmondo: A $400 GPS handheld that sold an estimated fewer than 25,000 units before its maker collapsed amid executives' criminal pasts and a Ferrari crash.
/failed-consoles/neo-geo-cd: SNK's CD console offered arcade-identical Neo Geo games at a quarter of the cartridge price, with a single-speed drive and minute-long loads.
/failed-consoles/neo-geo-pocket-color: The best-built handheld of its generation, with a clicking microswitched stick fighting fans still covet, killed by SNK's new owners.
/failed-consoles/nokia-n-gage: Nokia's taco-shaped phone and Game Boy rival, undone by awkward design, a $299 price and the infamous sidetalking call posture.
/failed-consoles/philips-cdi: A multimedia player that became a games machine almost by accident, notorious for four licensed Zelda and Mario games widely ranked among the worst.
/failed-consoles/rca-studio-ii: RCA's 1977 black-and-white console used built-in keypads instead of joysticks and was obsolete within the year against the Channel F and Atari VCS.
/failed-consoles/sega-32x: A Genesis add-on rushed out against the PlayStation and Saturn, which split Sega's own audience and confused buyers with too much hardware.
/failed-consoles/sega-neptune: A Genesis and 32X in one box for under $200, advertised in 1995 and cancelled that October; the pictured prototype was a non-working mock-up.
/failed-consoles/sega-nomad: A handheld Sega Genesis, sold only in North America just as Sega abandoned the Genesis, that drained six AA batteries in under three hours.
/failed-consoles/sega-pico: Sega's children's learning console, with book-like cartridges and a drawing surface: a success in Japan, a footnote in the West.
/failed-consoles/sega-saturn-west: A capable console undone in the West by a shock early launch, a $399 price and a dual-CPU design developers found nearly impossible to program.
/failed-consoles/tiger-game-com: A handheld sold as a gaming PDA with internet access and a touchscreen, none of which worked well, against the Game Boy Color.
/failed-consoles/tiger-r-zone: Tiger's $30 headset projected a red LCD game onto a mirror before one eye, launched in 1995 and routinely ranked among the worst consoles.
/failed-consoles/turbografx-16: NEC and Hudson's console dominated Japan as the PC Engine but found only modest success in North America against the NES and Genesis.
/famous-bugs/diablo-butcher-door: Behind a door on Diablo's second level waits the Butcher, a deliberate shock ambush with "Ahh, fresh meat!", not a bug.
/famous-bugs/goldeneye-invincibility-gli: Oddjob was so hard to hit in GoldenEye 007 multiplayer that "No Oddjob" became one of console gaming's best-known house rules.
/famous-bugs/gta-san-andreas-hot-coffee: Hot Coffee, a sex minigame left in San Andreas's code, was re-enabled by a mod and got the game re-rated Adults Only.
/famous-bugs/missingno-glitch-pokemon: MissingNo, a garbled sprite for invalid data, became a beloved bug, caught through the Old Man glitch and duplicating items.
/famous-bugs/mk-secret-character-blood-b: Reptile was hidden in arcade Mortal Kombat as a secret fight with near-impossible conditions, a deliberate bug-like secret.
/famous-bugs/mortal-kombat-blood-esrb: Mortal Kombat's Genesis blood code, entered on the Code of Honor screen, became a flashpoint in the 1993 violence hearings.
/famous-bugs/ocarina-of-time-unused-arwi: A working Star Fox Arwing sits dormant in Ocarina of Time's code, a debug object that flies and shoots at Link if triggered.
/famous-bugs/pokemon-mew-glitch-trainer-: A flaw in interrupted trainer battles let Pokémon players legitimately catch Mew, meant to be unobtainable without events.
/famous-bugs/pool-of-radiance-uninstalle: Uninstalling Pool of Radiance 1.0 deleted system files and left Windows unable to boot, a bug that shipped.
/famous-bugs/quake-quakeworld-desync: Early QuakeWorld's prediction and server timing made other players visibly warp, prompting key advances in online netcode.
/famous-bugs/smb-minus-world: Clipping through World 1-2's wall in Super Mario Bros. reaches "World −1", an underwater stage that loops endlessly.
/famous-bugs/superman-64-broken-release: Superman 64 buried its hero in fog and repetitive ring challenges with broken controls and collision, a byword for bad games.
/franchises/castlevania: Konami's gothic series from Hitoshi Akamatsu's 1986 original to Symphony of the Night, the Metroidvania and Koji Igarashi's departure.
/franchises/contra: Konami's run-and-gun series, from the 1987 arcade game and the NES version's 30-lives Konami Code to Contra III, Hard Corps and Contra 4.
