/franchises/donkey-kong: Donkey Kong introduced Mario as Jumpman, saved Nintendo of America, and returned with Rare's Donkey Kong Country; the series has sold over 65 million copies.
/franchises/dragon-quest: Horii, Toriyama and Sugiyama's RPG series: its Wizardry and Ultima roots, Dragon Quest III's truancy arrests and the myth of the weekday ban.
/franchises/final-fantasy: Hironobu Sakaguchi's last-ditch 1987 RPG became a series with a new world in every entry, Active Time Battle and more than 200 million copies sold.
/franchises/kings-quest: Roberta Williams's fairy-tale series began as a showcase for IBM's PCjr, and its pseudo-3D adventures built the reputation of Sierra On-Line.
/franchises/kirby: Masahiro Sakurai's series for beginners, from the white Kirby of the Game Boy box to Copy Abilities and The Forgotten Land, with 50 million games sold.
/franchises/mario: The best-selling game franchise of all time: from Jumpman in Donkey Kong to Super Mario Bros. and Super Mario 64, with over 900 million copies sold.
/franchises/mega-man: Capcom's six-person NES project became a series of 50-plus games. The rock-paper-scissors design, Inafune's art and the subseries that followed.
/franchises/metal-gear: Hideo Kojima's stealth series, from MSX2 hardware limits and The Great Escape to Metal Gear Solid's fame and 66.4 million units sold.
/franchises/metroid: Nintendo's solitary sci-fi series, from the 1986 twist of Samus Aran to Super Metroid, Retro Studios' Metroid Prime and MercurySteam's Metroid Dread.
/franchises/mortal-kombat: Midway's digitised fighter became the best-selling fighting game franchise, and concern over its Fatalities helped lead to the ESRB age ratings.
/franchises/pac-man: Toru Iwatani's Pac-Man sold about 400,000 cabinets by 1982, sparked over $1 billion of US merchandise and became America's most recognised game character.
/franchises/pokemon: Satoshi Tajiri's childhood insect collecting became Pokémon, a Game Boy game built on trading and now estimated to be the highest-grossing media franchise.
/franchises/resident-evil: Capcom's survival horror series, from the Sweet Home-inspired 1996 original to Resident Evil 4's reinvention and more than 218 million games sold.
/franchises/sonic: Sega's answer to Mario grew from a Yuji Naka tech demo. How Sonic took on Nintendo, struggled with 3D and reached 1.77 billion sales and downloads.
/franchises/street-fighter: Capcom's Street Fighter II created the modern competitive fighting game, earning over $10 billion; the series has sold 60 million units.
/franchises/tetris: Alexey Pajitnov's spare-time Soviet puzzle game, the tangled battle for its rights, the Game Boy's killer app and the disputed 520 million sales figure.
/franchises/tomb-raider: Toby Gard's Lara Croft and Core Design's 1996 hit, the annual sequels that burned out the team, and the Crystal Dynamics years: 100 million units sold.
/franchises/ultima: Richard Garriott's RPG series, from cloth maps and Ultima IV's Eight Virtues to the living world of Ultima VII and the hit MMORPG Ultima Online.
/franchises/zelda: Miyamoto and Tezuka's Zelda series set the action-adventure conventions of overworld and item dungeons, and has sold more than 150 million copies.
/game-engines/agi-sci: Sierra's AGI and SCI engines powered a decade of adventure games from King's Quest to Gabriel Knight and established the illustrated adventure.
/game-engines/build-engine: Ken Silverman's Build engine powered Duke Nukem 3D and Blood, adding room-over-room spaces and interactive environments to Doom's approach.
/game-engines/construct: Construct's event-sheet model let hobbyists build complete 2D games without writing code, a key accessible creation tool of the late 2000s.
/game-engines/freescape: Freescape powered 1987's Driller with solid 3D polygon worlds the player could explore freely, real 3D on 8-bit home computers.
/game-engines/gamemaker-engine: Mark Overmars' GameMaker, first released in 1999 as Animo, let non-programmers build games with drag-and-drop logic.
/game-engines/goldsrc: GoldSrc was Valve's heavily modified Quake engine for Half-Life, adding scripted events and AI that changed what shooters could express.
/game-engines/id-tech-1: The Doom engine brought binary space partitioning to real-time rendering, building a convincing 3D world from a 2D map on 1993 PCs.
/game-engines/id-tech-2: The Quake engine rendered fully polygonal worlds with real-time lighting and launched the online multiplayer scene of a generation.
/game-engines/id-tech-3: The first engine to render curved surfaces in real time, and the one that made the shader standard equipment in game development.
/game-engines/infinity-engine: BioWare's Infinity Engine combined pre-rendered backgrounds with real-time-with-pause combat to power Baldur's Gate and Planescape: Torment.
/game-engines/mugen-engine: A freeware 2D fighting engine whose fully customisable characters let fans build dream-match rosters mixing anyone with anyone.
/game-engines/quake-ii-engine: The Quake II engine added coloured lighting, better networking and a clean game DLL API, the most licensed shooter engine of the late 1990s.
/game-engines/renderware: Nicknamed "Sony's DirectX", RenderWare made the PlayStation 2 programmable and powered Grand Theft Auto III, Vice City and Burnout.
/game-engines/rpg-maker: RPG Maker gave non-programmers a tile editor, event scripting and ready-made battles, spawning decades of hobbyist and indie RPGs.
/game-engines/scumm: SCUMM was LucasArts' adventure engine, enabling the non-linear point-and-click games and "no dead ends" design of its classic adventures.
/game-engines/snes-mode-7: Mode 7 let the SNES rotate and scale a background plane in real time, producing the pseudo-3D roads and flight of early-1990s games.
/game-engines/source-engine: Valve's Source engine turned Havok physics into a gameplay mechanic and gave characters faces built on a taxonomy of human expression.
/game-engines/ultima-underworld-engine: Ultima Underworld's engine rendered a texture-mapped real-time 3D dungeon two months before Wolfenstein 3D, years ahead of the industry.
/game-engines/unreal-engine-1: Unreal Engine 1 debuted with Unreal in 1998: large environments, coloured lighting and a built-in scripting language that raised the visual bar.
/game-engines/z-machine: Infocom's 1979 virtual machine let one compiled game run on dozens of incompatible home computers, perhaps the most portable VM ever made.
/genres/action: Action games demand quick reflexes and real-time decisions, the broadest genre in gaming and the source of its visual and mechanical grammar.
/genres/mmorpg: The MMORPG gave MUDs graphics and thousands of simultaneous players; Ultima Online popularised the form in 1997 and EverQuest took it further.
/genres/racing: Racing games simulate vehicular competition, from Gran Trak 10's 1974 circuit to Pole Position's Fuji Speedway, driving arcade hardware forward.
/genres/rhythm: Rhythm games ask players to match inputs to music; born in late-1990s Japan, Dance Dance Revolution made play a public performance.
/genres/sports: Sports games simulate athletic competition; Pong (1972), a simplified table tennis, launched the entire video game industry.
/genres/strategy: Strategy and simulation games reward planning, resource management and systems thinking, from chess programs to Civilization, SimCity and X-COM.
/glitches/blj-super-mario-64: The backwards long jump on stairs in Super Mario 64 builds speed without limit, letting Mario pass through star doors and skip stars.
/glitches/bunny-hop-half-life: Jumping while strafing in Half-Life's Quake-derived engine keeps and exceeds running speed indefinitely, the bunny hop.
/glitches/corrupted-blood-wow: A World of Warcraft raid debuff escaped into its cities and became a virtual epidemic that killed thousands of characters.
/glitches/credits-warp-smw: Precise sprite tricks let players make Super Mario World run their own instructions, jumping straight to the ending.
/glitches/death-warp-zelda: Dying on purpose in Zelda returns Link to the dungeon entrance, a shortcut speedrunners use after grabbing an item deep inside.
/glitches/freeze-glitch-ocarina: Using Deku Nuts during certain sword moves in Ocarina of Time leaves Link's sword hitbox active, a continuous damaging attack.
/glitches/infinite-combo-sf2: Some move sequences in Street Fighter II: Hyper Fighting repeat indefinitely, keeping opponents stunned until they are defeated.
/glitches/metroid-secret-worlds: Exploiting Metroid's room scrolling lets Samus leave the map and roam "secret worlds" built from leftover data.
/glitches/minus-world-smb: Clipping through the wall at the end of World 1-2 in Super Mario Bros. reaches "World -1", an underwater stage that loops forever.
/glitches/ocarina-of-time-wrong-warp: Wrong warps corrupt Ocarina of Time's scene data to teleport Link, even straight into the credits, collapsing the world record.
/glitches/strafe-jumping-quake: Strafing sideways while moving forward and jumping in Quake let players accelerate past the intended top speed with every jump.
/glitches/super-mario-world-ace: Arbitrary code execution lets players program the SNES from inside Super Mario World, warping to the credits or running other games.
/hardware/amiga-ocs: The Amiga's three custom chips, and a coprocessor synchronised to the electron beam that made Amiga demos look impossible.
/hardware/atari-pokey: Atari's POKEY chip generated four voices of sound and read paddles and keyboards, the audio of the Atari 8-bit computers, Centipede and Gauntlet.
/hardware/genesis-ym2612: The Genesis paired Yamaha's YM2612 FM synthesis chip with a TI PSG, a warm, metallic sound that Yuzo Koshiro and others made genuinely musical.
/hardware/hudson-huc6270: The PC Engine's video chip, with 64 hardware sprites and 16 per line, designed by game developer Hudson Soft rather than a chip company.
/hardware/konami-vrc6: Konami's cartridge chip added three sound channels to the Famicom, giving the Japanese Castlevania III a richer score than the NES version.
/hardware/mos-6502: The 6502's $25 price in 1975 made personal computing affordable and powered nearly every major gaming platform of the late 1970s and early 1980s.
/hardware/mos-6581-sid: The SID chip gave the Commodore 64 the most sophisticated sound of any home computer of its era: three synthesis voices with programmable filters.
/hardware/mos-vic-ii: The Commodore 64's graphics chip: 16 colours, eight hardware sprites and raster interrupts that let programmers multiply sprites far beyond eight.
/hardware/motorola-68000: The 68000 powered the Amiga, Atari ST and Sega Genesis. Its clean instruction set made it a favourite processor for game development.
/hardware/n64-reality-coprocessor: The SGI-designed chip that handled all the Nintendo 64's graphics and audio, delivering console 3D that rivalled the workstations of its day.
/hardware/nes-apu: The NES audio chip packed five sound channels onto the CPU's die. Koji Kondo and Hirokazu Tanaka built iconic soundtracks within its tight limits.
/hardware/nintendo-dsp-1: A maths coprocessor in SNES cartridges that handled the 3D calculations behind Pilotwings and Super Mario Kart's pseudo-3D perspective.
/hardware/playstation-gpu: The PlayStation's GTE and GPU defined fifth-generation visuals and made texture-mapped polygon rendering the new standard for games.
/hardware/ricoh-rp2c02-ppu: The NES graphics chip: a memory-efficient tile-and-sprite design that gave the console its look and smooth scrolling ahead of most home hardware.
/hardware/sega-saturn-vdp: The Saturn's dual VDP chips gave it extraordinary 2D sprite performance just as the market moved to 3D, where the design was weakest.
/hardware/sharp-lr35902: The Game Boy's custom 8-bit CPU, a hybrid of the Intel 8080 and Zilog Z80 that ran on a modest clock and a famously frugal power budget.
/hardware/ti-tms9918: TI's 1979 video chip popularised hardware sprites and powered the ColecoVision, MSX and SG-1000; Sega's Master System chip grew from it.
/hardware/yamaha-opl-fm: Yamaha's OPL2 (9 FM channels) and OPL3 (18 channels) defined how DOS games sounded from the late 1980s through the 1990s.
/hardware/yamaha-v9938: The MSX2's video chip: a 512-colour palette, 128 KB of video RAM and drawing commands, behind the MSX2 Metal Gear and many Konami games.
/hardware/zilog-z80: Federico Faggin's Z80 powered the ZX Spectrum, Master System and Game Gear, inspired the Game Boy's CPU and became the 8-bit era's workhorse.
/imports/bahamut-lagoon-import: Square's 1996 Bahamut Lagoon combined grid tactics, party management and dragon raising on the Super Famicom, never released abroad.
/imports/dragon-quest-v-import: Dragon Quest V came out in Japan in 1992 and not in English until the 2009 DS remake, long called the series' best.
/imports/final-fantasy-v-import: Final Fantasy V came out in Japan in 1992 but not in English until 1999, seven years in which its Job System fascinated importers.
/imports/live-a-live-import: Square's 1994 Live A Live told seven self-contained chapters from prehistory to the far future, each drawn by a different artist.
/imports/lsd-dream-emulator-import: Based on an employee's dream diary, LSD (1998) is a Japan-only PlayStation game with no goals, just wandering surreal dreamscapes.
/imports/metal-gear-solid-demo-import: Metal Gear Solid's Japanese preview demo circulated among Western importers with a fervour far beyond its twenty minutes.
/imports/moon-remix-rpg-import: Love-de-Lic's 1997 anti-RPG Moon cast the player as the cleanup crew after a hero's rampage, unlocalised for over two decades.
/imports/neo-geo-aes-import: The Neo Geo AES launched in 1990–91 at $649 with $200 games, the defining object of early-1990s prestige gaming.
/imports/policenauts-import: Policenauts, Hideo Kojima's adventure about a cop revived after twenty-five years in space, came out in Japan on four platforms only.
/imports/puyo-puyo-import: Puyo Puyo was a Japanese puzzle hit that reached the West mainly in disguise, as Dr. Robotnik's Mean Bean Machine and Kirby's Avalanche.
/imports/radiant-silvergun-import: Treasure's Radiant Silvergun came out only in Japan and sold about 50,000 copies, making it one of the most expensive imports.
/imports/sakura-wars-import: Sakura Wars sold out within hours in Japan, but Sega doubted the West would embrace its strategy, dating sim and steampunk blend.
/imports/shenmue-import: Shenmue launched in Japan in December 1999 and in the West in November 2000, its reputation built by importers in between.
/imports/sin-and-punishment-import: Treasure's Sin and Punishment came out in Japan in 2000, late in the N64's life, and was never released in the West.
/imports/terranigma-import: Quintet's Terranigma reached Japan, Europe and Australia, but not North America, after Enix closed its US branch.
/imports/tokimeki-memorial-import: Tokimeki Memorial made the dating sim mainstream, sold a million and spawned an empire, but Konami never released it abroad.
/levels/battletoads-turbo-tunnel: Battletoads' Turbo Tunnel, a high-speed hoverbike gauntlet of memorised walls, is the definitive impossible NES level.
/levels/castlevania-clock-tower: Castlevania's Clock Tower distils the series: pixel-perfect platforming over moving gears and timed platforms under constant attack.
/levels/chrono-trigger-end-of-time: Chrono Trigger's End of Time, a single streetlight at the end of history, is an elegant hub for travel and character moments.
/levels/dkc-aquatic-ambiance: Donkey Kong Country's underwater stage stopped players for its graphics and for David Wise's advanced "Aquatic Ambiance".
/levels/doom-e1m1: Doom's E1M1 set the template for shooter level design in 1993, teaching navigation, combat pacing and resources in one compact map.
/levels/ecco-first-ocean: Ecco the Dolphin's opening ocean gives a sense of aquatic freedom and alienness unlike anything else in the 16-bit library.
/levels/ff6-opera-house: Final Fantasy VI pauses to stage an opera with a soprano aria on the SNES sound chip, then drops a giant octopus through the ceiling.
/levels/ff7-midgar-opening: Final Fantasy VII's Midgar opening is a compressed, brilliantly paced introduction to its world, systems and themes.
/levels/goldeneye-facility: GoldenEye 007's Facility, opening with Bond dropping into a bathroom, is a stealth-shooter masterclass and a multiplayer favourite.
/levels/half-life-2-ravenholm: Half-Life 2's Ravenholm takes your ammunition and leaves you in a zombie town with the gravity gun and a lot of saw blades.
/levels/half-life-black-mesa-inbound: Half-Life opens with a silent tram ride through Black Mesa, an unbroken first-person introduction that changed game storytelling.
/levels/mega-man-2-metal-man: Metal Man's stage in Mega Man 2 teaches the weapon economy through conveyor-belt platforming, with one of the era's catchiest themes.
/levels/ocarina-of-time-water-temple: Ocarina of Time's Water Temple, with rising and falling water and clumsy Iron Boots, is gaming's most notorious dungeon.
/levels/sf2-ken-stage: Ken's sunny San Francisco dock, with cheering sailors and cargo ships, is Street Fighter II's most visually iconic arena.
/levels/smb-world-1-1: Super Mario Bros.' World 1-1 may be gaming's most studied level, teaching every core mechanic through design alone, without text.
/levels/sonic-chemical-plant-zone: Chemical Plant Zone, Sonic 2's defining level, is a neon industrial gauntlet that pushed the Genesis to its visual limit.
/levels/sonic-green-hill-zone: Green Hill Zone took Yuji Naka close to a year, built and thrown away repeatedly, before it taught the world what Sonic felt like.
/levels/star-fox-64-corneria: Every Star Fox 64 run starts on Corneria, and how you play it decides where the game goes across its branching routes.
/levels/super-mario-64-bob-omb-battlefie: Bob-omb Battlefield had to teach the world 3D movement, and its open, spiralling mountain became the most influential 3D first level.
/levels/zelda-lttp-hyrule-castle: A Link to the Past's rainy midnight infiltration of Hyrule Castle is a benchmark opening that sets the tone and teaches the mechanics.
/localization/castlevania-ii-mistranslat: Simon's Quest's US localisation produced famous mistranslations, from "What a horrible night to have a curse" to misleading clues.
/localization/contra-nes-regional-names: Contra had three names in three regions, and Europe's Probotector replaced its human heroes with robots.
/localization/dragon-warrior-old-english: Nintendo renamed Dragon Quest as Dragon Warrior in 1989 and rewrote its script in mock-Elizabethan English, "thou hast" and all.
/localization/final-fantasy-tactics-tran: Final Fantasy Tactics' dense political tragedy came to English so badly translated that "breath" became "bracelet" throughout.
/localization/fire-emblem-western-debut: Fire Emblem's first Western release in 2003, the seventh Japanese game, dropped its number and was adjusted for newcomers.
/localization/mortal-kombat-blood-contro: In 1993 the SNES Mortal Kombat removed the blood while the Genesis kept it behind a code, handing Sega a decisive marketing win.
/localization/nintendo-content-guideline: Nintendo of America's late-1980s and early-1990s rules stripped crosses, blood, alcohol and religion from games before release.
/localization/pokemon-red-blue-western: Bringing Pokémon West meant renaming and trademarking all 151 creatures and reprogramming the games, a sweeping localisation.
/localization/punch-out-tyson-licensing: Mike Tyson's Punch-Out!! was reissued in 1990 as Punch-Out!! with a fictional final boss, Mr. Dream, after Tyson's licence expired.
/localization/revelations-persona-americ: Atlus USA moved Persona's story to America, renamed its cast and changed characters' skin and hair to look more American.
/localization/street-fighter-ii-regional: Street Fighter II's US release swapped three bosses' names so the Tyson-like boxer was not called M. Bison, a split that persists.
/localization/super-mario-bros-2-doki-do: America's Super Mario Bros. 2 was a reskinned Doki Doki Panic, because Nintendo of America found Japan's sequel too hard.
/localization/tecmo-bowl-real-players: Tecmo Bowl's NES version licensed real NFL players' names, the only NES football game with authentic rosters.
/localization/working-designs-localizati: Working Designs localised Japanese RPGs such as Lunar with lavish packaging, American humour and famously long delays.
/localization/zero-wing-all-your-base: Zero Wing's Mega Drive translation gave the world "All your base are belong to us", an internet phenomenon a decade later.
/lost-games/bio-force-ape: Bio Force Ape was a near-complete NES game by Seta, cancelled in 1991 and thought lost until a prototype surfaced at auction in 2010.
/lost-games/glover-2: The sequel to the N64's Glover was mostly finished when cancelled, reportedly because too many cartridges of the first had been made.
/lost-games/half-life-dreamcast: A finished Dreamcast port of Half-Life, with the exclusive Blue Shift expansion, cancelled weeks before release when Sega quit the console.
/lost-games/marble-madness-ii-marble-man: Atari's Marble Madness sequel added flight, invisibility and pinball, then died on location test in 1991 beside Street Fighter II.
/lost-games/primal-rage-2: Atari's Primal Rage sequel was cancelled after arcade location tests; two boards survive, and MAME now runs the lost game.
/lost-games/super-marios-wacky-worlds: A Nintendo-approved Super Mario World sequel for the CD-i, killed by the system's collapse at about 80% art and 30% code.
/lost-games/swordquest-airworld: Airworld was the planned final SwordQuest game, with a $150,000 prize contest, never developed after the 1983 crash.
/lost-games/ultima-escape-from-mt-drash: A VIC-20 Ultima in name only, sold on cassette in a few thousand copies and so obscure collectors long doubted it existed.
/magazines/ace-magazine: ACE was a multi-format British magazine that scored games out of 1,000 and drew a Predicted Interest Curve for each one.
/magazines/amiga-power: Amiga Power used the whole percentage scale, published a table showing rivals inflated their scores, and lost advertising for it.
/magazines/commodore-64-user: Commodore User launched in 1983, grew from programming tutorials into a games magazine and became CU Amiga in 1990.
/magazines/commodore-format: Future's Commodore Format arrived late in the C64's life, outsold Zzap!64 within two years and was the last of Britain's big 8-bit magazines.
/magazines/computer-and-video-games: Launched in 1981, Computer and Video Games is the UK's oldest games magazine, a reference through the Spectrum, Amstrad and Amiga eras.
/magazines/computer-gaming-world: Founded by Russell Sipe in 1981, Computer Gaming World was the first computer games magazine and covered PC gaming for 25 years.
/magazines/crash: Crash was the definitive 1980s ZX Spectrum magazine, famed for sharp reviews and Oliver Frey's covers, once Britain's top-selling computer title.
/magazines/edge: Edge is the UK's most critically rigorous games magazine: austere design, low scores for big games and games treated as serious design.
/magazines/electronic-games: Founded in 1981 by Bill Kunkel, Arnie Katz and Joyce Worley, Electronic Games was the first US magazine devoted to video games.
/magazines/electronic-gaming-monthly: EGM was the flagship US multiplatform magazine of the 1990s, known for its review grid and April Fools hoaxes that fooled a generation.
/magazines/game-informer: Game Informer began as FuncoLand's newsletter in 1991 and, tied to GameStop's loyalty scheme, became one of America's most-read magazines.
/magazines/game-players: Game Players was an early-1990s US magazine known for longer reviews, detailed strategy and a more analytical approach than its rivals.
/magazines/gamefan: GameFan was a cult US magazine of import coverage, full-page screenshots and an enthusiast voice that championed Japanese games early.
/magazines/gamepro: GamePro was a long-running US magazine for younger players, known for its ProReview format and mascot-heavy look.
/magazines/gamesmaster-magazine: Launched in 1993 with Channel 4's GamesMaster show, the magazine sold over 219,000 copies of issue one and outlived the show by 20 years.
/magazines/mean-machines: Mean Machines, CVG's console spin-off, became the defining irreverent voice of British 16-bit coverage in the Mega Drive and SNES era.
/magazines/next-generation: Next Generation, Edge's American sibling, was an intelligent, often controversial magazine that interrogated how games were made.
/magazines/nintendo-power: Nintendo's official US magazine was the strategy guide, preview source and brand ambassador for a generation of NES and SNES players.
/magazines/pc-gamer: PC Gamer is the longest-running PC games magazine, launched in the UK and US, which professionalised PC journalism and the demo disc.
/magazines/retro-gamer: Retro Gamer, launched in 2004, was the first commercial magazine devoted to retro games and survived its publisher's bankruptcy.
/magazines/sega-power: Future's Sega magazine began as S: The Sega Magazine in 1989, covered Master System to Saturn and ended as Saturn Power in 1998.
/magazines/sinclair-user: Sinclair User ran for eleven years and 134 issues, selling 96,000 copies a month at the height of the ZX Spectrum boom.
/magazines/super-play: Super Play was Future's British SNES magazine, revered for Japanese games, import RPGs and Wil Overton's manga-style covers.
/magazines/tips-and-tricks: Tips & Tricks was a US monthly entirely of cheat codes, passwords and strategy, the pre-internet clearinghouse for game secrets.
/magazines/your-sinclair: Your Sinclair swapped dry Spectrum coverage for anarchic, self-mocking humour, a tone that reshaped UK games journalism.
/magazines/zzap-64: Zzap!64, Newsfield's Commodore 64 sibling to Crash, was loved for its humour, exhaustive coverage and reviewers like Julian Rignall.
/manuals/chrono-trigger-manual: The Chrono Trigger manual showcased Akira Toriyama's character and monster art, making the booklet a keepsake in its own right.
/manuals/civilization-manual: MicroProse shipped Civilization with a reference encyclopedia, then built a hyperlinked second one into the game itself.
/manuals/contra-nes-manual: Konami's Contra manual leaned into action-movie style, with biographies for Bill Rizer and Lance Bean framing a military sci-fi story.
/manuals/dragon-warrior-manual: Dragon Warrior's manual, given free with Nintendo Power subscriptions, described Alefgard like a travel guide, from history to spells.
/manuals/earthbound-manual: EarthBound's North American release came with a 128-page Players' Guide as its manual, with scratch-and-sniff stickers and a walkthrough.
/manuals/falcon-4-manual: Falcon 4.0 shipped not with a manual but a library: a Flight Handbook, a Cadet's Guide and a Communications Handbook.
/manuals/final-fantasy-iv-manual: The SNES Final Fantasy II manual (Final Fantasy IV) gave Cecil, Rosa and Kain profiles that filled gaps left by the localisation.
/manuals/legend-of-zelda-nes-manual: The original Zelda manual gave players a full mythology, with Ganon's backstory, the Triforce's origin and a map that made Hyrule feel ancient.
/manuals/metal-gear-solid-manual: Metal Gear Solid printed Meryl's codec frequency on the CD case, and Psycho Mantis could only be beaten by moving the controller port.
/manuals/metroid-nes-manual: Metroid's manual called Samus Aran "he", keeping the twist intact for players who finished fast enough to learn she was a woman.
/manuals/pokemon-red-blue-manual: The manual that introduced the West to Pokémon, framing the journey through Professor Oak and the first choice of Bulbasaur, Squirtle or Charmander.
/manuals/secret-of-mana-manual: Secret of Mana's manual carried Hiro Isono's painterly cover of a vast tree and forest, one of the era's most beautiful game artworks.
/manuals/simcity-snes-manual: SimCity's 118-page SNES manual was partly written as advice from Dr. Wright, the game's invented city-planning adviser.
/manuals/wasteland-paragraph-book: Most of Wasteland's story was printed in a booklet of numbered paragraphs, including deliberate lies planted to catch cheats.
/merchandise/nintendo-cereal-system: Ralston's Nintendo Cereal System put two cereals in one box: a Super Mario Bros. corn cereal and a Zelda berry cereal.
/merchandise/pac-man-fever-craze: At the height of Pac-Mania, "Pac-Man Fever" reached the Billboard Top 10 and sold over a million copies amid a merchandising boom.
/merchandise/pokemon-anime-1997: The 1997 Pokémon anime, following Ash and Pikachu, was an instant phenomenon and a cornerstone of the franchise's global rise.
/merchandise/pokemon-burger-king-recall: Burger King's 1999 Pokémon promotion ended in a huge recall after its Poké Ball toy containers were linked to infant suffocation deaths.
/merchandise/pokemon-trading-card-game: The Pokémon Trading Card Game launched in Japan in 1996 and became a global phenomenon when Wizards of the Coast brought it West in 1998.
/merchandise/sonic-saturday-cartoon: DiC made two opposite Sonic cartoons in 1993: the comic Adventures of Sonic the Hedgehog and the darker, serialised Sonic the Hedgehog.
/merchandise/street-fighter-animated-fil: Group TAC's Street Fighter II animated film, directed by Gisaburo Sugii, was an unusually competent adaptation of the game.
/merchandise/street-fighter-ii-hasbro-fi: Hasbro's 1993 Street Fighter II figures were a G.I. Joe sub-line, 3.75-inch fighters built from recycled G.I. Joe moulds.
/merchandise/super-mario-bros-film-1993: The 1993 Super Mario Bros. film, with Bob Hoskins and John Leguizamo, was a critically derided box office disappointment.
/merchandise/super-mario-super-show: DiC's Super Mario Bros. Super Show mixed live-action Captain Lou Albano and Danny Wells as Mario and Luigi with NES-based cartoons.
/merchandise/tamagotchi: Bandai's Tamagotchi, a keychain egg whose creature died if ignored, sold its first 1.5 million US units in thirty-six hours.
/merchandise/tiger-electronics-lcd-games: Tiger's cheap single-game LCD handhelds put Sonic, Mortal Kombat and Street Fighter in kids' pockets with fixed-segment screens.
/merchandise/zelda-cdi-games: Philips' three CD-i Zelda games, including The Faces of Evil and The Wand of Gamelon, came from a failed Nintendo licensing deal.
/multiplayer/contra-nes-1988: Konami's 1988 NES Contra became the classic example of two-player co-op action: demanding, generous and built for two.
/multiplayer/halo-system-link-2001: Halo's System Link joined sixteen players on four Xboxes and four TVs, and a generation carried consoles to each other's houses.
/multiplayer/kirby-super-star-1996: Kirby Super Star's Helper system let a second player join at any time as an ally made from a copy ability.
/multiplayer/mario-party-n64-1998: Hudson Soft's Mario Party pitted four friends against each other in fifty-odd minigames, and its stick-spinning events hurt palms.
/multiplayer/nba-jam-1993: NBA Jam made basketball an over-the-top two-on-two arcade spectacle for four players, with real stars and "He's on fire!"
/multiplayer/phantasy-star-online-2000: Phantasy Star Online put four-player online action RPG play on the Dreamcast in 2000, with a phrasebook the game translated.
/multiplayer/street-fighter-ii-1991: Street Fighter II (1991) created the competitive one-on-one fighter: six buttons, motion-input specials and character matchups.
/multiplayer/super-mario-kart-1992: Super Mario Kart invented kart racing around two-player split screen, item combat and a Battle Mode made for pick-up-and-play.
/multiplayer/xband-modem-1994: The XBAND modem let Genesis and SNES owners play strangers over phone lines in 1994, with rankings, chat and matchmaking.
/packaging/atari-2600-painted-art: Atari 2600 boxes carried commissioned paintings of cinematic scenes for games that were abstract coloured blocks on screen.
/packaging/baldurs-gate-big-box-pc: Baldur's Gate came in a big box with five CDs, a map of the Sword Coast, a reference card and a thick manual, the peak of the PC big-box era.
/packaging/doom-shareware-box: Doom's free shareware episode was also sold in retail boxes, packaging that traded on Doom's fame to sell what players could legally copy.
/packaging/earthbound-big-box: EarthBound's oversized North American box held the game, a full-colour Player's Guide and scratch-and-sniff stickers of in-game enemies.
/packaging/fallout-big-box: Fallout's embossed box held a CD, a manual styled as a Vault-Tec survival guide and a great deal of air.
/packaging/final-fantasy-vii-black-box: Final Fantasy VII's North American release held three CD-ROMs in a black multi-disc case, a physical sign of the game's unusual scope.
/packaging/genesis-clamshell-case: Sega of America sold Genesis games in hinged black cases the size of a VHS tape, tougher than card and shelved like home video.
/packaging/halo-ce-big-box: Halo: Combat Evolved launched with the Xbox in November 2001 in a green-trimmed case with Master Chief on the cover, the console's defining image.
/packaging/infocom-feelies: Infocom packed its boxes with props such as evidence folders, pills, documents and coins that doubled as copy protection and became beloved.
/packaging/japanese-spine-cards: Japanese games shipped with a separate spine card carrying logo, price and barcode, often discarded and now key to a copy's value.
/packaging/monkey-island-dial-a-pirate: Monkey Island's copy protection was a cardboard wheel of pirate faces, a joke good enough that players kept the wheel for decades.
/packaging/myst-jewel-case: Myst's original jewel case showed a painted island on a dark background, a minimal cover that signalled mystery against busy box art.
/packaging/nes-black-box: Nintendo's 1985–1987 NES games shared the black box design: black backgrounds, enlarged in-game sprites and a series label.
/packaging/playstation-long-box: Sony launched the US PlayStation in second-hand tall cases and tried several worse ideas before settling on the jewel case.
/packaging/pokemon-red-blue-launch: Pokémon's North American launch used two identical boxes differing only in colour, making the purchase social and implying you needed both.
/packaging/shining-force-cd-jewel: Shining Force CD remade Sega's two Game Gear Shining Force Gaiden games for the Sega CD with an extra scenario, a rare Western RPG exclusive.
/packaging/snes-cardboard-box: American SNES games came in fragile card boxes with an internal tray that most owners threw away, now often worth more than the game.
/packaging/ultima-iv-feelies: Ultima IV came with a cloth map, a metal ankh and two books, objects that worked as copy protection, story and collector's items at once.
/packaging/wing-commander-joystick: Wing Commander's manual was Claw Marks, the onboard magazine of the TCS Tiger's Claw, introducing ships, pilots and the Kilrathi in fiction.
/peripherals/dreamcast-vmu: The Dreamcast's Visual Memory Unit was a memory card with an LCD screen, d-pad and buttons that doubled as a standalone handheld.
/peripherals/famicom-disk-system: Nintendo's rewritable Famicom disks and Japanese kiosks let players have a new game written onto an old disk for ¥500 in 1986.
/peripherals/gba-e-reader: A Game Boy Advance scanner that read dot patterns printed on cards, delivering NES games, minigames and levels before console downloads.
/peripherals/menacer: The Menacer was Sega's wireless infrared light gun for the Genesis, built to rival the Super Scope and usable as a rifle or a pistol.
/peripherals/n64-expansion-pak: A 4 MB module that doubled the N64's RAM. Donkey Kong 64, Majora's Mask and most of Perfect Dark could not run without it.
/peripherals/n64-rumble-pak: The Rumble Pak was the first mainstream accessory to make a console controller vibrate, a feature that became an industry standard.
/peripherals/nes-advantage: The NES Advantage was Nintendo's own arcade stick for the NES, with an 8-way joystick, large buttons and turbo fire.
/peripherals/nes-zapper: The NES Zapper was Nintendo's light gun, bundled with the console in North America and best known for Duck Hunt.
/peripherals/nintendo-64dd: The N64's magnetic disk drive: announced in 1995, delayed four years, sold only in Japan to subscribers and discontinued within fourteen months.
/peripherals/power-glove: The Power Glove was a motion-sensing NES controller worn like a glove, sold as the future of game control and remembered as barely functional.
/peripherals/power-pad: A floor mat of twelve pressure sensors for running and dancing in NES games, born as Bandai's Family Trainer; it sold half a million in North America.
/peripherals/rob-robotic-operating-buddy: R.O.B. was the NES Deluxe Set's robot, there to position the NES as a toy rather than a console after the 1983 crash.
/peripherals/sega-32x: The Sega 32X plugged into the Genesis and added two SH-2 processors, a stopgap 32-bit upgrade remembered as a great strategic miscalculation.
/peripherals/sega-activator: The Sega Activator was a floor ring of infrared beams that read body movement, fifteen years before motion gaming and unsuited to its games.
/peripherals/sega-netlink: A $199 28.8k modem that brought web browsing and online play to the Saturn in 1996, with players dialling each other directly in six games.
/peripherals/super-game-boy: A SNES cartridge with real Game Boy hardware inside, playing monochrome carts on a television with colour palettes and decorative borders.
/peripherals/super-scope: The Super Scope was Nintendo's wireless light gun bazooka for the SNES, an infrared successor to the Zapper that took six AA batteries.
/peripherals/vectrex: The Vectrex was an all-in-one home system with a built-in vector monitor, producing crisp geometric graphics unlike anything on a television.
/pixel-artists/akiman: Akiman's character designs defined Final Fight and Street Fighter II before he moved to anime mecha for Turn A Gundam and Code Geass.
/pixel-artists/akira-toriyama: Akira Toriyama's character designs gave Dragon Quest its instantly recognisable look, and his Chrono Trigger work is celebrated.
/pixel-artists/ayano-koshiro: Ayano Koshiro was character designer and artist at Ancient, the studio she founded with her brother Yuzo in the Mega Drive era.
/pixel-artists/bob-wakelin: Bob Wakelin airbrushed Ocean Software's covers, making cassette games look like blockbuster films, and designed Ocean's logo.
/pixel-artists/dan-malone: Dan Malone gave The Bitmap Brothers their metallic, riveted, industrial look, the visual identity of a small British studio.
/pixel-artists/henk-nieborg: Henk Nieborg's densely detailed Amiga backgrounds set the ceiling for 16-bit scenery, and he still makes pixel art professionally.
/pixel-artists/hiroshi-iuchi: Hiroshi Iuchi directed and art-directed Treasure's Radiant Silvergun and Ikaruga, a benchmark for the shoot 'em up's artistic ambition.
/pixel-artists/hiroshi-ono: Hiroshi Ono, "Mr. Dotman", drew Galaga, Dig Dug, Mappy and the Pac-Man cabinet art, defining Namco's golden-age look.
/pixel-artists/jim-sachs: Jim Sachs' hand-pixelled art for Defender of the Crown set such a high standard that his images were used to sell the Amiga.
/pixel-artists/kazuko-shibuya: Kazuko Shibuya turned Yoshitaka Amano's watercolours into Final Fantasy sprites and designed its title screen and blue menus.
/pixel-artists/mark-ferrari: LucasArts artist Mark Ferrari perfected EGA dithering and colour cycling, making rain fall and water ripple in still images.
/pixel-artists/naoto-ohshima: Naoto Ohshima designed Sonic the Hedgehog, a mascot of attitude and speed that defined Sega in the 16-bit era.
/pixel-artists/paul-reiche-iii: Paul Reiche III created Star Control's alien races, one of PC gaming's most celebrated science fiction universes.
/pixel-artists/yoshitaka-amano: Yoshitaka Amano's ethereal watercolour designs gave Final Fantasy its visual identity and brought fine art to game illustration.
/platforms/3do: The 3DO was a licensed console standard built by Panasonic, GoldStar and Sanyo, launched at $699.99 in 1993. Its hardware, games and history.
/platforms/amiga: The Commodore Amiga: custom chips, 4,096-colour HAM graphics, four-channel sampled sound and multitasking, and the home of Lemmings and Populous.
/platforms/apple-ii: Steve Wozniak's Apple II, sold from 1977, helped create the home computer market and sold about six million units. Its history, models and games.
/platforms/arcade: Arcade games from the golden age to the 1990s: US arcade revenue hit an estimated $8 billion in 1982, more than pop music and Hollywood films combined.
/platforms/atari-2600: The Atari 2600 popularised ROM cartridges and sold an estimated 30 million units; Space Invaders nearly doubled its installed base in 1980.
/platforms/atari-8bit: Atari's 400, 800, XL and XE computers had graphics superior to the Apple II's, custom ANTIC, GTIA and POKEY chips, and Star Raiders as a killer app.
/platforms/atari-jaguar: The Atari Jaguar: the "Do the math" 64-bit console, launched at $249.95 in 1993, with 63 licensed games and about 125,000 sold through 1995.
/platforms/atari-lynx: The Atari Lynx, the first handheld with a colour LCD: designed at Epyx, launched at $179.99 in 1989, with 71 games and eight-player linking.
/platforms/atari-st: The Atari ST: designed in five months under Jack Tramiel, launched in 1985, and a favourite of musicians thanks to its built-in MIDI ports.
/platforms/colecovision: The ColecoVision launched in 1982 with Donkey Kong, played Atari 2600 games through an expansion module, and sold over 2 million units.
/platforms/commodore-64: Guinness lists the Commodore 64 as the best-selling desktop computer model ever, at 12.5 to 17 million units. Its SID chip, history and games.
/platforms/dreamcast: The Dreamcast, Sega's last console and the first with a built-in modem, sold 9.13 million units before Sega quit hardware in 2001.
/platforms/famicom-disk-system: Nintendo's Famicom Disk System: rewritable Disk Cards, ¥500 Disk Writer kiosks, and the first home of Zelda, Metroid and Kid Icarus.
/platforms/game-boy: Gunpei Yokoi's Game Boy beat colour rivals on price and battery life; with the Game Boy Color it sold 118.69 million units. Its games and history.
/platforms/game-gear: Sega's Game Gear put Master System hardware behind a backlit colour screen. It sold about 14 million units but lasted only 3–5 hours on six AAs.
/platforms/genesis: The Sega Genesis (Mega Drive) had a two-year head start on the Super NES, fought it with Sonic and "Nintendon't", and sold 30.75 million units.
/platforms/msx: MSX, the shared home-computer standard from ASCII and Microsoft Japan, where Konami made Metal Gear, Vampire Killer and Nemesis. Its history and games.
/platforms/neo-geo: SNK's Neo Geo put its arcade hardware in a $649.99 home console. Fatal Fury, Samurai Shodown, King of Fighters and Metal Slug defined it.
/platforms/nes: The NES helped revive the US games industry after the 1983 crash. Launched as the Famicom in 1983, it sold 61.91 million units. Its games and history.
/platforms/nintendo-64: The Nintendo 64 brought Super Mario 64, Ocarina of Time and GoldenEye 007, but its cartridges pushed Square and Enix to PlayStation. 32.93M sold.
/platforms/pc-9801: NEC's PC-9801 held over 60% of Japan's PC market and shipped 18.3 million units, with its own world of strategy games, visual novels and Touhou.
/platforms/pc-dos: How the IBM PC and its DOS clones became the leading computer game platform, from CGA and the PC speaker to VGA, Sound Blaster and Doom.
/platforms/playstation: Sony's PlayStation grew from a cancelled Super NES add-on to the first platform to ship over 100 million units. Its games, launch and history.
/platforms/sega-master-system: Sega's Master System lost North America to the NES but thrived in Europe and Brazil, selling about 13 million units. Its games and history.
/platforms/sega-saturn: The Sega Saturn sold out on day one in Japan but stumbled in the West after a surprise $399 launch. It sold 9.26 million units. Games and history.
/platforms/snes: The Super NES: Mode 7, Super FX, a Sony-designed sound chip and 49.1 million units sold, the best-selling console of the 16-bit generation.
/platforms/turbografx-16: The PC Engine was once Japan's best-selling console and the first to use CD-ROM; as the TurboGrafx-16 it struggled in North America.
/platforms/virtual-boy: Nintendo's Virtual Boy used mirrors and red LEDs for stereoscopic 3D. It sold 770,000 units and 22 games before Nintendo quietly ended it in 1996.
/platforms/zx-spectrum: The ZX Spectrum launched at £125 in 1982, sold over five million units and helped build the UK games industry. Its history, hardware and games.
/ports/another-world: Éric Chahi built Another World nearly alone in polygons rather than sprites, which is why it ported to almost everything so well.
/ports/castlevania-sotn-saturn: The Japan-only Saturn Symphony of the Night added a second playable character, new areas and new enemies.
/ports/doom: Doom became the benchmark for shooter ports in the 1990s, its console conversions exposing the range of hardware and developer skill.
/ports/double-dragon: Double Dragon wrote the beat 'em up rulebook, yet its most-played home version cut the main draw: playing with a friend.
/ports/final-fight: Final Fight's SNES port lost a playable character, two-player co-op and some content to censorship, a textbook case of compromise.
/ports/goldeneye-007: GoldenEye 007, among the best-selling N64 games, went unported for over two decades because of a tangle of overlapping rights.
/ports/lemmings: Lemmings sold 55,000 copies on its first Amiga day and was ported to over 30 platforms, an estimated 15 million copies.
/ports/mortal-kombat: Mortal Kombat's 1993 ports sparked a violence debate when the SNES cut the blood and the Genesis restored it with a code.
/ports/nba-jam: NBA Jam's two-on-two basketball reached nearly every mid-1990s platform, the 16-bit versions keeping its energy and hidden characters.
/ports/out-run: Sega's Out Run was one of the most ported arcade games of the late 1980s, with results from impressive to barely recognisable.
/ports/pac-man-atari-2600: Pac-Man's rushed 1982 Atari 2600 port is one of gaming's most notorious conversions and a contributor to the 1983 crash.
/ports/prince-of-persia: Jordan Mechner's rotoscoped platformer began on the Apple II and was ported widely, its fluid animation surviving every conversion.
/ports/sonic-the-hedgehog-8bit: Sonic's 8-bit Game Gear and Master System versions were new games designed around weaker hardware, not direct ports.
/ports/space-harrier: Space Harrier's hydraulic cabinet threw the player around; every home version had to recreate a game whose best feature could not be copied.
/ports/space-invaders-2600: Space Invaders on the Atari 2600 was the industry's first killer app, quadrupling sales of the console it ran on.
/ports/street-fighter-ii: Street Fighter II's move from CPS-1 arcade hardware to home consoles was a console-war landmark, each version a benchmark of its machine.
/ports/strider: Strider's Mega Drive conversion won Game of the Year, while its home computer versions spawned a sequel Capcom had nothing to do with.
/ports/teenage-mutant-ninja-turtles-arca: Konami's four-player TMNT brawler was a beloved coin-op; its home ports, especially on NES, showed the sacrifices conversion required.
/ports/tetris-licensing: Tetris went from a Soviet institute to the world's most-played game through a fierce licensing dispute that gave Nintendo handheld rights.
/ports/wolfenstein-3d: Nintendo's rules turned Wolfenstein 3D's Nazis into the "Staatmeister" and mutant rats of a Master State, with almost no blood.
/producers/bernie-stolar: Bernie Stolar built the PlayStation's US third-party lineup, then ran Sega of America and controversially ended the Saturn.
/producers/don-mattrick: Don Mattrick led EA's studios through its most dominant decade, then ran Xbox through the 360's success and the Xbox One's launch.
/producers/gabe-newell: Gabe Newell left Microsoft after Doom convinced him it was missing the point of the internet, then built Half-Life and Steam.
/producers/hayao-nakayama: Hayao Nakayama drove Sega to 60% of the US console market with the Genesis, then lost that lead by abandoning it early for the Saturn.
/producers/howard-lincoln: Howard Lincoln was Nintendo of America's legal strategist and later chairman through the console wars and the violence hearings.
/producers/jim-levy: Jim Levy brought the record industry's credited, royalty-earning artist to video games at Activision, inventing third-party publishing.
/producers/ken-kutaragi: Ken Kutaragi, "Father of the PlayStation", secretly built a sound chip for Nintendo, was nearly fired, then built the PlayStation.
/producers/ken-williams: Ken Williams built Sierra On-Line from a kitchen-table operation into an adventure game empire run from the Sierra Nevada foothills.
/producers/lincoln-spector: Lincoln Spector was a PC game critic and tech journalist whose PCWorld and InfoWorld columns shaped how Americans judged PC software.
/producers/masayuki-uemura: Masayuki Uemura designed the Famicom and Super Famicom, consoles that together sold over 110 million units worldwide.
/producers/minoru-arakawa: Minoru Arakawa founded Nintendo of America and turned a struggling arcade distributor into the force behind the NES launch.
/producers/nolan-bushnell: Nolan Bushnell co-founded Atari in 1972, made Pong and built Atari into a billion-dollar company before selling it to Warner.
/producers/peter-main: Peter Main led Nintendo of America's marketing at its peak, making Nintendo the dominant brand in American toy and entertainment retail.
/producers/ray-kassar: Ray Kassar ran Atari at its peak and called its programmers "towel designers", prompting the founding of Activision.
/producers/satoru-iwata: Satoru Iwata rescued HAL Laboratory from near-bankruptcy, then led Nintendo through the DS and Wii, a gamer at heart.
/prototypes/castlevania-64-early-builds: Early Castlevania 64 builds were more ambitious than the shipped game, with a larger castle, more characters and a different camera.
/prototypes/chrono-trigger-original-conc: Chrono Trigger's early concepts from the 1992 Dream Team of Sakaguchi, Horii and Toriyama had a different world and battle system.
/prototypes/doom-alpha-0-4: Doom's early-1993 alphas had a different monster roster, another HUD and weapons heavily reworked before the December release.
/prototypes/earthbound-nes-prototype: Nintendo of America nearly finished an English NES Mother, titled EarthBound, in 1989–90, then cancelled it; it was later released officially.
/prototypes/final-fantasy-vii-2d-prototy: Final Fantasy VII was first planned for the Super Famicom, with an early story set in New York, before moving to PlayStation and 3D.
/prototypes/goldeneye-007-prototype-arca: GoldenEye 007 began as an on-rails shooter like Virtua Cop before Rare's small team made it free-roaming and added multiplayer.
/prototypes/half-life-2-2003-leak: A German programmer broke into Valve's network out of curiosity, and an unfinished Half-Life 2 leaked more than a year before release.
/prototypes/halo-macworld-1999-reveal: The Halo Steve Jobs showed at Macworld 1999 was an open-world third-person Mac game on the Myth engine, unlike the Xbox shooter.
/prototypes/mega-man-rockman-japanese-pr: Akira Kitamura's team considered names such as Rainbow Man before settling on Rockman, and the finished game lacked passwords.
/prototypes/ocarina-of-time-spaceworld-9: A 3D Zelda was first shown in short demos at Shoshinkai and Space World in 1995 and 1996, with an older-looking Link.
/prototypes/resident-evil-4-hookman: An early Resident Evil 4 was supernatural horror in which an infected Leon hallucinated a hook-armed ghost climbing out of a painting.
/prototypes/sonic-needlemouse-prototype: Before Sonic had a name, Sega called him "Mr. Needlemouse", as Naoto Ohshima's hedgehog beat a rabbit and an armadillo to be mascot.
/prototypes/star-fox-snes-super-scope-or: Star Fox grew out of Argonaut Software's 3D experiments on Nintendo hardware, which led to the Super FX chip.
/publishers/acclaim-entertainment: Acclaim was a leading NES and SNES-era publisher of arcade ports and licences such as Mortal Kombat, NBA Jam and Turok.
/publishers/accolade: Founded by two Activision founders, Accolade won the court case that made reverse-engineering a games console legal in the United States.
/publishers/atari-classic: Nolan Bushnell and Ted Dabney's Atari created the games industry with Pong and defined home consoles with the 2600 before its collapse.
/publishers/capcom: Named after "Capsule Computers", Capcom built its own arcade hardware and made fighting games and survival horror commercial genres.
/publishers/codemasters: Founded by two teenage brothers who had already earned £200,000 from budget games, Codemasters became a long-lived British studio.
/publishers/electronic-arts: Trip Hawkins founded EA in 1982 to credit developers like rock musicians, and it grew into the world's largest third-party publisher.
/publishers/epyx: Epyx made Summer Games, Impossible Mission and Chip's Challenge on Atari and Commodore 64, and co-designed the Atari Lynx.
/publishers/gremlin-graphics: A Sheffield publisher that made Monty Mole, Thing on a Spring, Lotus Turbo Challenge and Zool, and the first fully 3D football game.
/publishers/hudson-soft: Hudson Soft created Bomberman and Adventure Island and was the first third-party developer on the Famicom.
/publishers/infocom: Infocom wrote the finest interactive fiction of its era, including Zork, Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy and Trinity.
/publishers/interplay: Brian Fargo's Interplay created Fallout, published Baldur's Gate and Descent and housed Black Isle before financial collapse.
/publishers/konami: A jukebox repair business from Osaka that became one of the most consistently excellent publishers of the 8- and 16-bit eras.
/publishers/lucasarts: George Lucas's games division became the finest adventure studio with Monkey Island and Grim Fandango, and made definitive Star Wars games.
/publishers/mastertronic: Mastertronic sold £1.99 games through newsagents, became one of Britain's biggest software houses and brought the Master System to the UK.
/publishers/midway-games: Midway brought Pac-Man to America and made Mortal Kombat, NBA Jam and Defender before a long decline ended in bankruptcy.
/publishers/psygnosis: Psygnosis was Britain's defining high-end Amiga publisher, known for Roger Dean covers, before Sony bought it and it made WipEout.
/publishers/sierra-on-line: Ken and Roberta Williams' Sierra invented the graphic adventure with Mystery House and led it with King's Quest and Space Quest.
/publishers/snk: SNK sold a home console that was literally arcade hardware, at $649 with $200 cartridges, and never pretended it was for everybody.
/publishers/sunsoft: Sunsoft became one of the most admired NES publishers with Blaster Master, Batman, Journey to Silius and Gimmick!, famed for its music.
/publishers/taito: Taito launched the global game industry with Space Invaders in 1978, then made Bubble Bobble, Arkanoid, Elevator Action and Qix.
/publishers/tecmo: Founded in 1967 to make cleaning equipment, Tecmo created Bomb Jack, Rygar, Ninja Gaiden, Tecmo Bowl and Dead or Alive.
/publishers/thq: THQ began as a toy company in 1990, became a giant of licensed games and went bankrupt in 2012 with its franchises auctioned off.
/publishers/us-gold: US Gold began importing American games to Britain and became the country's leading publisher of arcade conversions.
/regional/bionic-commando-nazi-censorshi: Japan's Bionic Commando openly fought Nazis; the NES version removed the imagery and names but kept the story structure intact.
/regional/dragon-quest-dragon-warrior: Japan's phenomenon Dragon Quest became Dragon Warrior in North America in 1989, with improvements and a guide, and sold poorly.
/regional/final-fantasy-numbering: Square released six Final Fantasy games in Japan before the US had three, so the American numbering skipped to match.
/regional/final-fight-snes-censorship: The SNES Final Fight cut a playable character, a stage and two-player mode, altered a character's gender and renamed two others.
/regional/fire-emblem-western-exclusion: Fire Emblem began in Japan in 1990; it took seven games, twelve years and a Smash Bros. Melee cameo for Nintendo to localise it.
/regional/kirby-box-art-eyebrows: Kirby's 1992 US box showed him as a pale white blob, since the Game Boy screen was monochrome, and the colour was later corrected.
/regional/link-to-the-past-religious-cen: Nintendo of America's rules stripped crosses, hexagrams and priests from A Link to the Past, turning churches into sanctuaries.
/regional/metal-gear-nes-port: Metal Gear was an MSX2 game; the June 1988 NES version was a different port built in about three months by a separate team.
/regional/panel-de-pon-tetris-attack: Panel de Pon, Intelligent Systems' 1995 puzzle game starring fairies, came West in 1996 as Tetris Attack with its own world removed.
/regional/pokemon-red-green-vs-red-blue: Japan's original Pokémon were Red and Green; the West's Red and Blue were built on the revised Japanese Blue with better sprites.
/regional/secret-of-mana-woolsey-transla: Secret of Mana was cut down for cartridge after the SNES CD died, and Ted Woolsey had thirty days to translate it into a tiny text box.
/regional/street-fighter-ii-port-history: Street Fighter II reached SNES, Genesis, PC Engine, Game Boy, Amiga, DOS and more over six years, and each port differed.
/retro-revival/axiom-verge: Axiom Verge was made by one developer over seven years beside a full-time job, deeply engaging with Super Metroid's design.
/retro-revival/bloodstained-curse-of-the: A Kickstarter stretch goal became Curse of the Moon, a tribute to Castlevania III so faithful IGN called it near-imitation.
/retro-revival/cave-story: One person spent five years making Cave Story's code, art, music and design, proving a lone developer could make a retro classic.
/retro-revival/celeste: Celeste is a brutally precise platformer in the 8-bit tradition, built on one rule: it must feel hard but always fair.
/retro-revival/cuphead: Two brothers remortgaged their homes to finish Cuphead, animated cel by cel in the style of 1930s cartoons.
/retro-revival/fez: Fez is a flat 8-bit platformer in a secretly 3D world: rotate the view ninety degrees and the geometry rearranges.
/retro-revival/hollow-knight: Two Australians built Hollow Knight, a vast hand-drawn underworld that owes its bones to Super Metroid and redefined the genre.
/retro-revival/hotline-miami: Hotline Miami fused top-down one-hit kills with a neon 1989 Miami aesthetic and an electronic soundtrack.
/retro-revival/la-mulana: La-Mulana was built to look and sound exactly like a 1986 MSX game, with some of the hardest puzzles in modern gaming.
/retro-revival/mega-man-9: Capcom made Mega Man 9 in 2008 with NES-era graphics and sound as a deliberate design method, not emulation.
/retro-revival/shovel-knight: Shovel Knight followed strict NES-style rules on palettes, tiles and audio, and became one of the best-reviewed games of its year.
/retro-revival/stardew-valley: Stardew Valley was one developer's four-year rebuild of classic Harvest Moon, and became one of the best-selling indie games.
/retro-revival/streets-of-rage-4: Streets of Rage 4 arrived twenty-six years after the third, made by three small European studios with a core team of about five.
/retro-revival/the-messenger: The Messenger, a Ninja Gaiden homage, switches from 8-bit to 16-bit graphics partway and uses the switch for time travel.
/retro-revival/undertale: Undertale was made by one person in GameMaker, using SNES JRPG style to question everything retro RPGs take for granted.
/retro-revival/vvvvvv: VVVVVV strips the platformer down to gravity flipping, with no jumping, in a Commodore 64 style made by a single developer.
/rom-hacks/ace-attorney-investigations-2: Capcom never localised Ace Attorney Investigations 2, so fans translated it, for years the only English version of the series' acclaimed entry.
/rom-hacks/doom-community-wads: Landmark Doom II megawads from three decades of community level design, from Erik Alm's work to John Romero's own return.
/rom-hacks/ff6-brave-new-world: Brave New World is a Final Fantasy VI rebalance that stops its customisation system from turning every character into the same one.
/rom-hacks/final-fantasy-iv-namingway-ed: The Namingway Edition restores Final Fantasy IV's Japanese script and cut content to the US Final Fantasy II and lets you rename everyone.
/rom-hacks/final-fantasy-v-rpge-translat: RPGe's Final Fantasy V was the first RPG fully translated by fans, made by amateurs and inspiring a generation of translators.
/rom-hacks/kaizo-mario-world: T. Takemoto's 2007 Super Mario World hack, with invisible blocks and post-goal traps, gave its name to the whole kaizo genre of ultra-hard ROM hacks.
/rom-hacks/metroid-super-zero-mission: Super Zero Mission rebuilds Super Metroid as a retelling of the original Metroid, with Zero Mission's physics in the SNES engine.
/rom-hacks/mother-3-fan-translation: A professional translator spent two years on a free English Mother 3, then offered Nintendo the script at no cost for an official release.
/rom-hacks/ocarina-of-time-randomizer: The Ocarina of Time randomizer shuffles every chest, song and gift into random places, guaranteeing by logic the game stays completable.
/rom-hacks/pokemon-brown: Pokémon Brown replaced Kanto with the new region of Rijon, with new maps, plot and types, the template for ambitious Pokémon hacks.
/rom-hacks/seiken-densetsu-3-translation: For a generation, this fan patch was the only English Seiken Densetsu 3, beating the game's text compression years before an official release.
/rom-hacks/street-fighter-ii-nes: An unlicensed NES port of Street Fighter II: Champion Edition by a Taiwanese pirate developer, grotesquely degraded but shipped anyway.
/rom-hacks/super-metroid-redesign: Super Metroid: Redesign rebuilds Zebes nearly twice the original's size, with new physics and areas that add hours of play.
/rom-hacks/zelda-alttp-randomiser: The A Link to the Past randomiser shuffles every item in Hyrule, an endlessly replayable hunt with a big competitive community.
/rom-hacks/zelda-parallel-worlds: Parallel Worlds rebuilds A Link to the Past with a new overworld, dungeons and story at extreme difficulty, one of the most ambitious SNES hacks.
/sales-figures/arcade-peak-1982: US arcades earned an estimated $8 billion in 1982, more than Hollywood's box office and the record industry combined.
/sales-figures/crash-of-83: North America's game market fell from $3.2 billion in 1983 to about $100 million by 1985, a 97% collapse.
/sales-figures/final-fantasy-vii-sales: Sony marketed a Japanese RPG nobody thought had a Western audience, and Final Fantasy VII established both the genre and the PlayStation.
/sales-figures/genesis-units: The Sega Genesis sold 30.75 million units, Sega's most successful console and the only time it matched Nintendo.
/sales-figures/gta-san-andreas-sales: GTA San Andreas sold 17.33 million copies on the PlayStation 2 alone, the best seller on the best-selling console.
/sales-figures/nes-units: The NES sold 61.9 million units, reviving a North American market that the 1983 crash had cut from $3.2 billion to about $100 million.
/sales-figures/nintendo-64-units: The N64 sold 32.93 million units, beaten by the PlayStation but the most influential commercial disappointment in Nintendo's history.
/sales-figures/nintendo-ds-units: Nintendo called the two-screened DS an experiment, not a Game Boy successor, and it became the best-selling handheld ever.
/sales-figures/playstation-2-units: The PlayStation 2 sold around 160 million units over thirteen years, the best-selling home console in history.
/sales-figures/playstation-units: The original PlayStation sold 102.49 million units, the first console past 100 million and the end of Nintendo and Sega's dominance.
/sales-figures/pokemon-franchise-sales: Pokémon games had sold over 440 million units by 2022, second only to Mario among video game franchises.
/sales-figures/snes-units: The Super Nintendo sold 49.1 million units and produced the deepest run of acclaimed games of any console generation.
/sales-figures/sonic-franchise-sales: The Sonic the Hedgehog franchise reached 150 million units by 2011, the best-selling series of the Genesis era.
/sales-figures/street-fighter-ii-sales: Street Fighter II and its revisions sold over 15 million home copies across SNES, Genesis and PC.
/sales-figures/super-mario-bros-sales: Super Mario Bros. sold about 40.24 million copies, the best-selling single-platform game until Wii Sports overtook it.
/sales-figures/the-sims-sales: The Sims had no goal, score or way to win, yet it overtook Myst as the best-selling PC game in barely two years.
/sales-figures/wii-sports-sales: Wii Sports, a bundled tech demo, became the best-selling single-platform game ever and the reason many households owned a Wii.
/sequels/baldurs-gate-ii: BioWare answered every criticism of the first Baldur's Gate, and with the engine done, spent its time on content.
/sequels/castlevania-symphony-of-the-nig: Symphony of the Night swapped linear platforming for a non-linear RPG in a sprawling castle that doubles in size mid-game.
/sequels/diablo-ii: Diablo II turned a one-dungeon game into a genre with skill trees, sockets, runes, item rarities and mercenaries.
/sequels/donkey-kong-country-2: Donkey Kong Country 2 refined the original in every way, with Dixie Kong's helicopter spin reshaping its level design.
/sequels/doom-ii: Doom II brought larger maps, the dominant Super Shotgun and new enemies that pushed the original's combat to its limits.
/sequels/dragon-quest-iii: Dragon Quest III added party building, class changes and day and night, then revealed itself as a prequel. It sold a million on day one.
/sequels/final-fantasy-vii: Final Fantasy VII went 3D, swapped medieval fantasy for industrial sci-fi and brought the series to a Western mainstream audience.
/sequels/grand-theft-auto-iii: GTA III moved the series from top-down 2D to a full 3D city and invented the modern open-world game.
/sequels/majoras-mask: Built in fifteen months on Ocarina of Time's engine, Majora's Mask became Nintendo's strangest, darkest and most radical game.
/sequels/mega-man-2: Mega Man 2 refined the original into a near-perfect action-platformer with eight Robot Masters and balanced weapons.
/sequels/metal-gear-2-solid-snake: Kojima made Metal Gear 2 after someone else made a sequel without him; it held nearly every idea later praised in Metal Gear Solid.
/sequels/metal-gear-solid-2: Metal Gear Solid 2 swapped Solid Snake for an unknown rookie after its prologue, a deliberate betrayal that made it postmodern.
/sequels/phantasy-star-ii: Phantasy Star II moved to the Mega Drive on the largest console cartridge yet, dropped 3D dungeons and killed a main character.
/sequels/resident-evil-2: Resident Evil 2 moved from a mansion to a zombie-filled city with linked scenarios for Leon and Claire.
/sequels/sonic-the-hedgehog-2: Sonic 2 added the Spin Dash, introduced Tails as a co-op companion and delivered longer, more branching levels.
/sequels/street-fighter-ii: Street Fighter II created the competitive fighting game: six buttons, distinct characters and frame data that rewards mastery.
/sequels/streets-of-rage-2: Streets of Rage 2 gave every fighter special moves, added a wrestler and a rollerblading kid, all set to Yuzo Koshiro's club-music score.
/sequels/super-mario-bros-3: Super Mario Bros. 3 invented the overworld map, a power-up inventory and movement-changing suits that the series built on for decades.
/sequels/super-metroid: Super Metroid refined Metroid's exploration into a masterwork of environmental storytelling, atmosphere and movement.
/sequels/ultima-iv-quest-of-the-avatar: Ultima IV had no villain; the goal was to become a good person, and the game watched how you behaved.
/sequels/zelda-link-to-the-past: A Link to the Past returned Zelda to top-down exploration at a scale and depth that made the original look like a prototype.
/sound-chips/amiga-paula: Paula, the Amiga's audio chip, played four 8-bit PCM channels by DMA in 1985, letting composers use sampled instruments and tracker music.
/sound-chips/atari-pokey: POKEY gave Atari's 8-bit computers four sound voices while also handling the keyboard, serial communication and paddle controllers.
/sound-chips/ay-3-8910: The AY-3-8910's three square-wave voices and noise channel sounded in the ZX Spectrum 128, Amstrad CPC, MSX and Atari ST.
/sound-chips/ensoniq-5503-doc: The Apple IIGS used Ensoniq's synthesiser wavetable chip, designed by SID creator Bob Yannes, the best-sounding home computer of 1986.
/sound-chips/game-boy-dmg-apu: The Game Boy's four sound channels, two pulse waves, a wavetable and noise, defined portable game audio and founded the chiptune movement.
/sound-chips/konami-scc: Konami's SCC wavetable chip, built into its MSX cartridges, added five channels and produced some of the finest 8-bit game music.
/sound-chips/konami-vrc6: Konami's VRC6 added two pulse channels and a sawtooth to the Famicom, giving the Japanese Castlevania III its celebrated soundtrack.
/sound-chips/oki-msm6295: The MSM6295 was the arcade industry's workhorse sample chip, streaming ADPCM drums, speech and effects on countless 1990s boards.
/sound-chips/playstation-spu: The PlayStation's sound chip mixed 24 channels of compressed CD-quality samples with hardware reverb, beside a CD drive that could stream music.
/sound-chips/ricoh-rf5c164: The RF5C164 gave the Sega CD eight channels of PCM sample playback from 64 KB of wave RAM, beyond anything the Mega Drive could do.
/sound-chips/ti-lpc-speech-chips: TI's speech chips began in the Speak & Spell and gave Atari's arcade games their voices, from Star Wars to the narrator of Gauntlet.
/sound-chips/ti-sn76489: The SN76489, a simple three-voice PSG with noise, was the Master System's sound chip and the Mega Drive's secondary one.
/sound-chips/yamaha-opl2-opl3: The OPL2 and OPL3 FM chips powered PC game audio from the late 1980s to the mid-1990s and defined a generation of DOS soundtracks.
/sound-chips/yamaha-ym2203: Yamaha's YM2203 (OPN) combined three FM and three square-wave channels, the layered sound of Japanese home computers in the 1980s.
/sound-chips/yamaha-ym2612: The YM2612 gave the Mega Drive six channels of 4-operator FM synthesis, the sound Yuzo Koshiro turned into some of the 16-bit era's finest music.
/sound-effects/asteroids-heartbeat: Asteroids had no music or sound chip, yet its two alternating, quickening notes raised players' pulses more than most soundtracks.
/sound-effects/blue-shell-mario-kart: The rising shriek of an incoming Spiny Shell in Mario Kart 64 became the series' most emotionally charged audio cue.
/sound-effects/doom-shotgun: Doom's punchy shotgun, built by Bobby Prince from real recorded sound, helped make realistic recordings the norm for game weapons.
/sound-effects/earthbound-smaash: EarthBound's cartoonishly huge "SMAAASH!!" critical-hit crash is one of the fondest-remembered attack sounds in RPGs.
/sound-effects/mario-jump: The rising chirp when Mario jumps in Super Mario Bros., a short pulse-wave sweep, is among the most-heard sound effects in gaming.
/sound-effects/metal-gear-solid-alert: Metal Gear Solid's sharp alert stab, with a red exclamation mark over the guard, is gaming's most recognised alert sound.
/sound-effects/mortal-kombat-finish-him: Mortal Kombat's "Finish Him!" and "Fatality!" turned its gruesome finishing moves into a cultural event.
/sound-effects/pac-man-death: The descending whimper when a ghost catches Pac-Man accompanied perhaps the most-repeated death of gaming's first decade.
/sound-effects/pacman-waka: Pac-Man's "waka waka" was built by Namco's Toshio Kai from alternating square waves, imitating a mouth at work.
/sound-effects/pong-beep: Bushnell wanted a cheering crowd and Dabney boos, but Allan Alcorn used tones already in the circuit, creating Pong's beep.
/sound-effects/quake-shotgun: Quake's deep shotgun, designed by Trent Reznor, processed real recorded gunfire through industrial music techniques.
/sound-effects/sega-chant: The sung "Se-ga" opening Sonic the Hedgehog took about an eighth of the cartridge and cost a planned Sonic animation.
/sound-effects/sonic-ring: Sonic's ring chime, by Dreams Come True's Masato Nakamura, is one of the most frequently heard sound effects of 16-bit gaming.
/sound-effects/space-invaders-march: Space Invaders' four descending notes speed up as the aliens advance, gaming's first interactive, tension-building soundtrack.
/sound-effects/street-fighter-2-ko: Street Fighter II's announcer, "Round One… Fight!", "K.O." and "Perfect", gave fighting-game victory its definitive voice.
/sound-effects/street-fighter-hadouken: Ryu and Ken's shouted "Hadouken!" in Street Fighter II became the most imitated voice sample in gaming history.
/sound-effects/super-mario-1-up: Super Mario Bros.' six-note 1-Up jingle is gaming's most universally understood signal of something good happening.
/sound-effects/tetris-line-clear: Hirokazu Tanaka's bright line-clear sound in Game Boy Tetris turned clearing a row into a perfectly judged audio reward.
/sound-effects/zelda-item-discovery: Zelda's five-note item fanfare captures the feeling of discovery so well it became gaming's universal sound for finding something.
/soundtracks/actraiser-ost: Yuzo Koshiro's sweeping ActRaiser score convinced the industry the SNES could do orchestral music and stunned rival composers.
/soundtracks/castlevania-sotn-ost: Michiru Yamane's Symphony of the Night score spans baroque harpsichord, heavy rock, jazz fusion and Renaissance styles across 48 tracks.
/soundtracks/chrono-trigger-ost: Chrono Trigger's score, mostly by Yasunori Mitsuda with Nobuo Uematsu finishing it, is widely called the best of the 16-bit era.
/soundtracks/doom-ost: Bobby Prince's 32-track Doom soundtrack of metal, industrial and ambient pieces drew on existing metal songs to build its own identity.
/soundtracks/ducktales-ost: Capcom's DuckTales, from the Mega Man team, has a Moon stage theme often called the finest piece of 8-bit music ever written.
/soundtracks/earthbound-ost: Keiichi Suzuki and Hirokazu Tanaka's 153-track EarthBound score samples pop, country, surf rock and more, the SNES's most eclectic.
/soundtracks/final-fantasy-vii-ost: Nobuo Uematsu's four-disc Final Fantasy VII score brought the series to 3D and gave us "One-Winged Angel", its first track with vocals.
/soundtracks/legend-of-zelda-ost: Koji Kondo's eight-track Legend of Zelda score introduced the overworld theme and title fanfare that define the series' sound.
/soundtracks/mega-man-2-ost: Takashi Tateishi's Mega Man 2 score is the most beloved NES soundtrack outside Nintendo's own, Dr. Wily's stage above all.
/soundtracks/ocarina-of-time-ost: Koji Kondo's Ocarina of Time score is one the player performs: twelve melodies played on the controller that open doors and bend time.
/soundtracks/secret-of-mana-ost: Hiroki Kikuta's debut Secret of Mana score blends progressive rock, ambient and world music, among the SNES's most atmospheric.
/soundtracks/silent-hill-2-ost: Akira Yamaoka's Silent Hill 2 score fuses ambient dread, industrial noise and trip-hop melody, among horror gaming's most complex.
/soundtracks/street-fighter-ii-ost: Yoko Shimomura wrote most of Street Fighter II's character themes, the most iconic fighting game soundtrack of the 16-bit era.
/soundtracks/super-mario-64-ost: Koji Kondo's Super Mario 64 score swapped tight 2D loops for airy, jazz-inflected themes to match Mario's first open 3D world.
/soundtracks/super-mario-bros-ost: Koji Kondo's Super Mario Bros. score, thirteen tracks on the NES chip, is the most widely recognised game music ever written.
/soundtracks/super-metroid-ost: Kenji Yamamoto and Minako Hamano's Super Metroid score is among the most influential ambient game soundtracks ever made.
/soundtracks/tetris-game-boy-ost: Hirokazu Tanaka's Game Boy Tetris turned a Russian folk song into gaming's most recognisable music, with Bach and Tchaikovsky alongside.
/speedrun-techniques/oot-bottle-adventur: A bottle on the B button makes Ocarina of Time write item values outside the inventory, conjuring almost any item.
/speedrun-techniques/oot-wrong-warp: A bottle trick in Gohma's room confuses Ocarina of Time's loading so the Deku Tree's blue warp sends child Link to Ganon's Castle.
/speedrun-techniques/pokemon-rby-trainer: Flying away the moment a trainer starts a battle corrupts Pokémon Red and Blue's encounter data, letting players catch Mew.
/speedrun-techniques/sm64-parallel-unive: Accelerate Mario until his position overflows and he reaches parallel universes, copies of a level outside the map.
/speedrun-techniques/smb1-warp-zones: Super Mario Bros.' hidden warp zones in Worlds 1-2 and 4-2 skip ahead, and the 4-2 warp to World 8 anchors modern any% routes.
/speedrun-techniques/super-metroid-x-ray: Stuck in a wall, Samus toggles the X-Ray Scope to be shunted upward five pixels at a time, climbing out of bounds.
/speedruns/battletoads-any: Battletoads' speedrun needs frame-perfect inputs through the Turbo Tunnel and Clinger Winger, which stop even experienced runners.
/speedruns/castlevania-any: Castlevania speedruns turn on frame-perfect stairs, sub-weapon damage tricks and precise enemy routing through a punishing NES game.
/speedruns/doom-e1-any: Doom speedrunning began within weeks of its December 1993 release, as players traded demos, one of the oldest speedrun communities.
/speedruns/final-fantasy-i-any: Final Fantasy I speedruns skip most of the game with a dungeon-loading glitch and encounter manipulation to finish in under an hour.
/speedruns/goldeneye-agent-dam: GoldenEye 007 has one of the most competitive individual-level speedrun scenes, contested across twenty missions and three difficulties.
/speedruns/mega-man-2-any: Mega Man 2 speedruns optimise the boss weapon order, sliding and room-transition glitches in a beloved NES platformer.
/speedruns/mike-tysons-punchout-any: Punch-Out!! speedruns demand frame-perfect reactions to every opponent, and Tyson's fight needs a precise punch in its first second.
/speedruns/ocarina-of-time-any: Ocarina of Time any% uses arbitrary code execution to reach the credits from the first dungeon in under seven minutes.
/speedruns/quake-e1-any: Quake speedrunning built on Doom's community and pushed its bunny-hopping 3D movement physics to their mathematical limit.
/speedruns/sonic-the-hedgehog-any: A speedrun of a game already about speed, whose record barely moves after thirty years of optimising the route.
/speedruns/super-mario-64-16-star: Super Mario 64's 16-star run, collecting just enough stars for the final battle, is the most contested category in N64 speedrunning.
/speedruns/super-metroid-any: Super Metroid any% is one of the SNES's most technical speedruns, mastering mockball and wall jumps to finish in about forty-one minutes.
/strategy-guides/donkey-kong-country-nin: Nintendo's Donkey Kong Country guide tried to capture Rare's pre-rendered 3D look in full-colour print.
/strategy-guides/doom-official-strategy-: Jonathan Mendoza's 1994 Doom guide from Sybex, one of many books that year as Doom became a publishing category of its own.
