/strategy-guides/earthbound-players-guid: EarthBound's Player's Guide, boxed with scratch-and-sniff stickers and written with suburban absurdism, is the most distinctive RPG guide.
/strategy-guides/final-fantasy-ultimania: Japan's Ultimania books treat games as scholarship, with artwork, interviews and lore, and have sold over 12 million copies.
/strategy-guides/final-fantasy-vii-offic: Brady Games' massive Final Fantasy VII guide covered its sixty-plus hours and became one of the best-selling strategy guides ever.
/strategy-guides/gamefaqs: GameFAQs, founded in November 1995, gave away volunteer-written walkthroughs for free and dismantled the printed strategy guide industry.
/strategy-guides/mario-mania-players-gui: Mario Mania was the first Nintendo Player's Guide devoted to one game, Super Mario World, with a history of Mario's career.
/strategy-guides/myst-prima-official-str: Prima's Myst guide sold over 1.25 million copies, the company's first bestseller and proof guides could reach beyond gamers.
/strategy-guides/nintendo-power-super-ma: Nintendo Power's Super Mario Bros. 3 coverage was the definitive English guide and set the template for magazine-format strategy guides.
/strategy-guides/ocarina-of-time-players: A 128-page companion to Ocarina of Time with a signed preface from Shigeru Miyamoto and a fold-out map of Hyrule.
/strategy-guides/pokemon-red-blue-offici: Nintendo's official Pokémon guide for the 1998 North American launch became one of the best-selling strategy guides in history.
/strategy-guides/street-fighter-ii-turbo: The official Street Fighter II Turbo SNES guide's move lists and combos became the template for 1990s fighting game guides.
/strategy-guides/super-metroid-nintendo-: Nintendo's Super Metroid player's guide used in-world photography and atmosphere that matched the game's isolation and mystery.
/strategy-guides/versus-books: A GameFan editor refused a cut of a guide line he pitched quit to found Versus Books, whose Perfect Guides fans rated above official ones.
/strategy-guides/zelda-link-to-the-past-: Nintendo's full-colour official guide to A Link to the Past covered every dungeon and secret and became the SNES guide gold standard.
/studios/bioware: Three medical doctors in Edmonton quit medicine to make RPGs, and BioWare became the most celebrated Western RPG studio.
/studios/bungie: Alex Seropian founded Bungie in a Chicago apartment and recruited programmer Jason Jones to build the studio behind Marathon and Halo.
/studios/cinemaware: Cinemaware sold games as playable movies, from swashbucklers to 1950s creature features, built for the Amiga.
/studios/core-design: Derby's Core Design spent eight years making solid British games before Tomb Raider made it briefly the country's most famous developer.
/studios/double-fine: Tim Schafer founded Double Fine after eleven years at LucasArts writing and directing Day of the Tentacle, Full Throttle and Grim Fandango.
/studios/ensemble-studios: Ensemble Studios made Age of Empires mainstream historical strategy, was bought by Microsoft for $100 million and closed eight years later.
/studios/factor-5: Founded in Cologne by ex-Rainbow Arts staff, Factor 5 made Turrican II and later pushed Nintendo hardware hard with Rogue Squadron.
/studios/game-arts: Game Arts made Thexder and Silpheed, then the Lunar and Grandia RPGs that gave Sega's CD and Saturn some of their best-loved games.
/studios/hal-laboratory: HAL nearly went bankrupt in the early 1990s and was saved by Nintendo with Satoru Iwata in charge. Its next game was Kirby's Dream Land.
/studios/id-software: id Software was born when four Softdisk employees secretly built a game on company time and left together to found their own studio.
/studios/intelligent-systems: Nintendo's programming unit became a creator with Famicom Wars and Fire Emblem, then Paper Mario, WarioWare and Panel de Pon.
/studios/looking-glass: Looking Glass grew out of Blue Sky Productions, the team that built an immersive 3D dungeon game for Origin Systems.
/studios/naughty-dog: Andy Gavin and Jason Rubin founded Naughty Dog as teenagers and kept it alive for a decade until Crash Bandicoot became PlayStation's mascot.
/studios/neversoft: Neversoft was weeks from running out of money when Activision gave it a failing project that became Tony Hawk's Pro Skater.
/studios/rare: Tim and Chris Stamper taught themselves machine code in a Leicestershire farmhouse and built Rare into a game empire.
/studios/sega-am2: Yu Suzuki's AM2 drove Sega's arcade dominance for eighteen years, from Super Scaler games to the 3D fighter and Shenmue.
/studios/sensible-software: Jon Hare and Chris Yates made Wizball, Mega-Lo-Mania, Sensible Soccer and Cannon Fodder before selling to Codemasters in 1999.
/studios/sonic-team: The Sega team that created Sonic the Hedgehog, took its name, and made NiGHTS into Dreams, Sonic Adventure and Phantasy Star Online.
/studios/team17: Team17 formed in 1990 from a British Amiga publisher and a Swedish team, dominated the Amiga charts and found a lasting hit in Worms.
/studios/technos-japan: Founded by three Data East veterans, Technos invented the modern beat 'em up with Renegade and perfected it with Double Dragon.
/studios/toaplan: A small Tokyo studio whose decade of arcade shooters shaped the genre, and whose 1994 collapse seeded the companies that carried it on.
/studios/treasure: Founded by Konami veterans tired of sequels, Treasure became renowned as a small, uncompromising and technically fearless action studio.
/studios/valve: Two former Microsoft employees put over $1 million of their savings into Valve, which redefined the shooter and then PC distribution.
/studios/westwood: Brett Sperry and Louis Castle founded Westwood in Las Vegas in 1985; it defined real-time strategy with Dune II and Command & Conquer.
/urban-legends/aerith-revival: Aerith's death in Final Fantasy VII was so shocking that players traded methods to revive her. None of them worked.
/urban-legends/atari-et-burial: Atari's buried E.T. cartridges were thought an urban myth for decades until a 2014 dig in a New Mexico landfill confirmed them.
/urban-legends/blowing-on-cartridges: Blowing into NES cartridges to fix them was a universal ritual, but the moisture actually made the connection problem worse.
/urban-legends/cartridge-blowing-ritual: Blowing into faulty cartridges was a near-universal childhood ritual, discovered independently everywhere, and it never really worked.
/urban-legends/konami-code-origin: Kazuhisa Hashimoto created the Konami Code to help himself test the NES Gradius, and it became gaming's most famous cheat.
/urban-legends/l-is-real-2401: A blurry inscription in Super Mario 64's courtyard was read as "L is real 2401", supposed proof of a hidden Luigi who never appeared.
/urban-legends/lara-croft-nude-code: The "Nude Raider" code supposedly unlocked a naked Lara Croft in Tomb Raider; it spread widely but never existed in any release.
/urban-legends/lavender-town-syndrome: Lavender Town Syndrome is a creepypasta claiming Pokémon's original Lavender Town music made Japanese children ill.
/urban-legends/mew-under-truck: The rumour that Mew hid under the truck near the S.S. Anne in Pokémon Red and Blue spread across playgrounds worldwide. It was false.
/urban-legends/missingno: MissingNo is a real glitch Pokémon in Red and Blue, born from memory handling, famous for duplicating items and its corrupted look.
/urban-legends/nuclear-gandhi: The story that an integer overflow made Gandhi nuke-happy in the original Civilization is popular, but the bug never existed.
/urban-legends/pokemon-creepypasta: Pokémon Lost Silver and other haunted-cartridge tales are crafted horror fiction so convincing that many readers believe them.
/urban-legends/polybius: Polybius is the legend of a 1981 Portland arcade cabinet, supposedly government-run, that caused amnesia and insomnia in players.
/voice-actors/akio-otsuka: Akio Otsuka voices Solid Snake in Japanese; Kojima's team modelled Snake's movements and smoking habit on the actor himself.
/voice-actors/charles-martinet: Charles Martinet voiced Mario from 1991 to 2023, from trade-show demos to 100 games recognised by Guinness, before becoming Mario Ambassador.
/voice-actors/david-hayter: David Hayter voiced Solid Snake from 1998 to 2012, a raspy, stoic baritone that became the definitive voice of stealth action.
/voice-actors/grey-delisle: Grey DeLisle has over two thousand roles in animation and games, a range so wide most players have heard her without knowing.
/voice-actors/jen-taylor: Jen Taylor voices two icons at opposite ends of gaming: Nintendo's Princess Peach and Halo's AI companion Cortana.
/voice-actors/jennifer-hale: Jennifer Hale, widely seen as games' finest dramatic voice actress, is best known as Commander Shepard in the Mass Effect trilogy.
/voice-actors/lani-minella: Lani Minella voiced male and female characters across hundreds of 1990s and 2000s games, pioneering women in male roles.
/voice-actors/mark-hamill: Mark Hamill's Joker in Batman: The Animated Series and the Arkham games set the standard for theatrical villain work in games.
/voice-actors/michael-ironside: Michael Ironside gave Splinter Cell's Sam Fisher a gravel-voiced, restrained professionalism that made stealth feel adult.
/voice-actors/norio-wakamoto: Norio Wakamoto's thunderous baritone made him Japanese gaming's voice of gods, emperors and villains, including M. Bison.
/voice-actors/paul-eiding: Paul Eiding voiced Colonel Roy Campbell, whose weary, paternal codec calls gave Metal Gear Solid its conscience.
/voice-actors/shigeru-miyamoto-voice: Shigeru Miyamoto created Mario but never voiced him; actors including Peter Cullen preceded Charles Martinet in the role.
/voice-actors/simon-templeman: Simon Templeman was Kain for seven years and five Legacy of Kain games, a sardonic performance worthy of a classical villain.
/voice-actors/steve-downes: Steve Downes has voiced Master Chief since Halo: Combat Evolved in 2001, the stoic voice that defined the Xbox.
/voice-actors/tara-strong: Tara Strong is one of the most prolific voice actors in games and animation, from Bubbles and Harley Quinn to Twilight Sparkle.
/voice-actors/tim-curry: Stage and screen star Tim Curry brought theatrical menace to games early, headlining Gabriel Knight: Sins of the Fathers in 1993.
/voice-actors/tony-jay: RSC veteran and Disney's Judge Frollo, Tony Jay's raspy baritone voiced some of the late 1990s' most commanding game villains.
/years/1971: 1971 was the first year of the commercial video game industry: Nutting Associates shipped Computer Space, and Galaxy Game was installed at Stanford.
/years/1973: In 1973 Atari launched Pong nationally and a wave of clones started the first video game fad, while Sega and Taito released Japan's first coin-op video games.
/years/1974: In 1974 arcades moved beyond Pong: Kee Games' Tank was the year's best-selling arcade game, Atari's Gran Trak 10 used ROM, and Namco bought Atari Japan.
/years/1975: In 1975 the first microprocessor games appeared: Midway's Gun Fight, Atari's eight-player Indy 800, home Pong at Sears and early PLATO role-playing games.
/years/1976: In 1976 Atari shipped Breakout, Coleco's Telstar sold a million units, Fairchild released the first cartridge console and Adventure began interactive fiction.
/years/1979: In 1979 the arcade boom gathered pace: Atari released Asteroids and Lunar Lander, and Namco brought full colour to Galaxian.
/years/1981: American arcades took an estimated $4.8 billion in 1981, the golden age's peak, and Donkey Kong introduced Mario.
/years/1983: The North American video game market collapsed in 1983 and 1984, losing an estimated $3 billion and nearly ending home gaming.
/years/1986: If 1985 established the NES, 1986 defined what it was for, with The Legend of Zelda and Metroid introducing open exploration.
/years/1989: Nintendo launched the Game Boy in Japan in April 1989, and bundling it with Tetris abroad was one of gaming's great decisions.
/years/1992: Mortal Kombat reached arcades in 1992 and homes in 1993, and its digitised gore and Fatalities triggered US Senate hearings.
/years/1993: id Software released Doom as shareware in December 1993 and redefined what a game could be: terrifying, kinetic and networked.
/years/1995: The PlayStation launched in North America in September 1995 at $299, undercutting the Saturn's surprise $399 price by $100.
/years/1996: The Nintendo 64 launched in Japan in June 1996 with Super Mario 64, a game unlike anything that came before it.
/years/1999: Sega launched the Dreamcast in North America on 9 September 1999, the biggest launch day in gaming to that point.
/years/2000: Sony launched the PlayStation 2 in 2000, while older consoles had Perfect Dark, Majora's Mask, Final Fantasy IX and Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 2.
/years/2001: The sixth console generation reached full strength in 2001, with Nintendo's GameCube arriving in Japan on 14 September.
